Introduction

How to Use This Guide

This guide is intended for developers of BuildCraft Community Edition addons and integrations. It describes the public contracts of API 2.1.0 for BCCE 8.0.24, their use in game systems, and the responsibilities that remain with the addon.

Start with your first integration, then proceed to the game system you need. The built-in reference contains public types and their declarations. The relevant chapters distinguish what the contract provides from what the standard game runtime actually does.

The chapters are grouped into five parts: integration fundamentals; machines and energy; transport and logistics; world, robots, and presentation; and maintenance. After learning the general rules for registration, operation modes, and context lifetimes, you can read individual chapters independently.

Four Questions to Ask Before Implementing Anything

For any integration, first determine what is registered, who executes the behavior, who owns the resources, and what survives saving the world. These questions are connected, but they are not the same. A machine type describes its structure; a host runs components; ports transfer resources; and a codec handles data. Confusing these responsibilities causes more problems than forgetting a particular class name.

Terminology

Java contract names and some established English technical terms are used throughout this guide. They have the following meanings.

TermMeaning in This Guide
RuntimeThe running API implementation that provides services and manages their lifecycles.
BackendA concrete executor of a public contract, such as a bridge to standard transport or loader-native storage.
HostThe entity responsible for running the components of a particular game object. It creates and activates them, invokes the specified callbacks, and manages persistence and synchronization within its contract.
Descriptor / type definitionData describing an extension: its stable ID, properties, and references to components or factories. Registering a definition does not create a Minecraft block.
Callback / handlerAn addon method invoked by BCCE at a specific execution point. Its context and permitted operations depend on that point.
PortA resource-access contract for insertion, extraction, and optionally inspection. Obtaining a port does not reserve any resources.
ViewAccess to state through a restricted interface. If a view exposes a port, permitted operations are governed by the port's own contract.
CodecA conversion between a runtime value and its serialized representation, with explicit error reporting.
PayloadThe contents of persisted or transmitted state. The schema belongs to the particular data type.
SnapshotA value captured for a specific read, save, or registry generation. An immutable wrapper does not necessarily make nested objects immutable.
FreezeThe point at which type registries are frozen. Their contents can no longer be changed by ordinary registration.
ReloadA new attempt to assemble and publish a set of definitions for an already registered type. It is not another type-registration step.
ProvenanceInformation about a definition's origin: owner, source, and priority. Used to resolve conflicts and diagnose problems.
Native / built-inAn existing BCCE game mechanic connected through an API adapter.
FixtureA small API consumer used to validate specific contracts. It may demonstrate only registration or one operation, and need not be a complete playable mod.

Reading the Examples

The examples assume that the required Minecraft objects and loader dependencies have already been registered. Complete standalone Java classes are explicitly labeled. Shorter snippets demonstrate an operation in the stated context; they do not invent an enclosing mod, fields, or event handlers merely to show one call.

IDs such as examplemod:* and example:*, fuel parameters, and task names are illustrative. The shared API uses ResourceLocation; chapter one explains the vanilla naming differences in 26.X and the corresponding builds. The examples do not promise binary compatibility between Minecraft versions.

Each topic chapter provides links to source declarations and implementations, which can be opened on this page. Where the public contract allows more than the installed game runtime implements, the practical limitations are explained in the relevant chapter.

I. Integration Fundamentals

01Purpose and Scope of the API

BCCE API is intended for developers of BuildCraft Community Edition addons and integrations. It lets you describe new kinds of pipes, machines, and robot tasks; add recipes and resource-processing rules; connect automation to permission systems; and expose data to interfaces. You should already know Java, the basics of Minecraft modding, and your chosen loader's lifecycle. Knowledge of BuildCraft internal classes is not required.

The supported public Java contracts live in the buildcraft.api.v2 namespace. BuildCraftApi.VERSION is 2.1.0, while the mod version is 8.0.24. The API version identifies the extension interface; the BCCE version identifies the game-mod release. Do not confuse the two.

The API spans 43 packages and 438 Java files, including the root package description. The main guide groups them by developer task. The separate reference maps each source file to its chapter and lets you inspect exact declarations of methods, nested types, and constants. You do not need to read the entire reference in sequence.

What Counts as a Public Contract

A Java class being declared public does not automatically make it part of the API. For example, classes in buildcraft.lib.internal and buildcraft.transport.internal, Tile* implementations, and the internal expression API support BCCE itself. Importing them ties an addon to implementation details. The supported addon boundary is defined by the buildcraft.api.v2 namespace, not by whether the compiler can resolve a class from the JAR.

That boundary has three main elements:

ElementPurposeExample
Registered typeDescribes an extension with a stable ID; exists independently of any particular block in the worldPipeType, MachineType, RobotTaskType
ServicePerforms operations, discovers objects, or manages a domainPipeService, EnergyService, SchematicService
View or contextProvides constrained access to the state of a particular object or operationPipeView, MachineView, WorldAccessContext

A pipe type is not a pipe already placed in the world. A pipe view does not grant permission to rewrite its internal graph arbitrarily. A lookup service does not guarantee that a suitable object exists at the given position. These distinctions underpin all subsequent integrations.

In many areas, BCCE provides a standard implementation of lifecycles and persistence, while the addon supplies components and handlers. Elsewhere, a public type describes a capability whose in-game implementation must still be provided by the addon or a specific module. You must therefore distinguish the existence of a class, a registered ID, and actual working game behavior.

Loader Independence

The shared API contracts do not import Forge, NeoForge, Fabric, or Minecraft client classes. They do not expose Capability, loader-specific FluidStack, DeferredRegister, or loader-specific transaction objects. For example, shared code uses FluidPort and FluidVolume, while the platform adapter bridges to native storage.

The API is still coupled to Minecraft. Its signatures include ItemStack, BlockPos, Direction, Level, resource identifiers, and other vanilla types. Their names and methods, the Java toolchain, mod metadata formats, and loader integration points can differ between game versions. The shared API design therefore simplifies maintenance across builds but does not promise a single binary JAR for every Minecraft version.

BCCE 8.0.24 supports the following build configurations:

MinecraftLoaderJavaBuild family
1.19.2Forge17old
1.20.1Forge17old
1.21.1NeoForge211.21.X
1.21.11NeoForge211.21.X
26.1.2NeoForge2526.X

This table lists BCCE 8.0.24 build configurations. The presence of preparatory Fabric directories does not imply Fabric support: those targets are absent from targets.properties. Before releasing an addon, confirm that a build exists for its intended Minecraft version and loader.

Shared Java code uses net.minecraft.resources.ResourceLocation. In the Minecraft 26.X family, the corresponding vanilla type is called Identifier. BCCE adapts shared sources to the target platform; external addon code must use the Minecraft names and signatures of its own target version.

Availability Checks

ApiVersion indicates the contract version. ApiFeatureSet lets you check a specific capability and its level. ModuleService reports which modules are physically loaded. Finally, ApiRuntime.service(...) returns a specific available service.

A feature level is not a completion percentage or a Minecraft version. For example, BuildCraftFeatures.PIPES at level 2 declares a particular transport API surface. Working with a pipe still requires the transport service, a loaded world, and a suitable object. Further limits of individual services are covered in their chapters.

For required dependencies, use requireService or BuildCraftApi.service so missing components are detected explicitly. For optional integrations, use runtime.service(key) and handle an empty Optional. Checking a feature is useful before using newer contracts, but it is no substitute for looking up the service.

For example, the Builders module installs the SCHEMATICS and LIBRARY services during bootstrap. The presence of a runtime feature does not mean a module has already installed its service at an arbitrary early point. This is ordinary modular initialization before freeze, not a promise that service will return a deferred result.

I. Integration Fundamentals

02Differences from the Original BuildCraft API

The main change in BCCE is the boundary between addon dependencies and BuildCraft internals. The original API offered integration points alongside base game-object classes, loader capabilities, network callbacks, and global registries. BCCE API v2 defines a separate contract layer: extension descriptors, services, restricted object views, explicit operations, and state formats.

This comparison uses the original BuildCraft/BuildCraftAPI branch 8.0.x-1.12.2 (commit b12940daa173f6b3fa7482eb7fcc2f210a018208). It applies to that original API lineage and should not automatically be generalized to every BuildCraft release. BCCE combines the BC8 foundation with restored BC7 mechanics, including robots and construction.

What the Original API Already Had

Original BuildCraft had an extensive extension system: pipe registration, behavior factories, MJ interfaces, triggers and actions, schematic adapters, and recipe and fuel integrations. PipeDefinition already used ResourceLocation; IMjReceiver already supported simulation; MjAPI already used microjoules and supported RF conversion; and the registry package already included data-reload contracts. None of these ideas should be presented as having originated in BCCE.

What changed is how these ideas fit together and what constitutes a supported addon dependency. Original PipeFlow, for instance, exposed pipe references, NBT, network payloads, Forge ICapabilityProvider, and gameplay methods together. BCCE separates those concerns into shared contracts and provides domain-specific tools for each.

Comparison of Integration Models

AreaOriginal API, selected lineageBCCE API 2.1
Entry pointMultiple static holders: PipeApi, BuildcraftFuelRegistry, StatementManager, MjAPIBuildCraftApi and typed service and registry keys
Loader dependencyForge capabilities and loader types appear in public contractsShared signatures use API-owned ports and vanilla types; loader adapters reside in the implementation
Pipe extensionFactories and subclassing public PipeBehaviour / PipeFlow, with direct ties to the holder and networkPipeType, components, rules, attachments, and separate definitions for custom flows/behaviors
RegistriesSome domains expose mutable maps and replaceable static servicesType registries with stable IDs, owners, aliases, and freeze; services have domain-specific policies
StateDomain-specific NBT formats; robot API associates a registered name with a Java class instantiated using reflectionPersistentType, codecs, schema migration, and typed/unknown payloads where the host supports them
Resource transferDifferent historical result formats, boolean simulate, and loader-specific interfacesShared OperationMode, explicit item/fluid/MJ transfer results, and a separate external-energy contract
Automation contextFakePlayer provider and context tied to individual game objectsAutomationActor, operation target and kind, and a permission service recording decision provenance
StatementsString tags, generic parameter maps, readers, and runtime interfacesRegistered TriggerType, ActionType, and ParameterType, schemas, and dedicated presentation contracts
Client-side dataTextures, network callbacks, and some client dependencies intermingled with semanticsDeclarative presentation contracts and typed channels; client implementation remains in BCCE
Version supportStrong coupling to the relevant Minecraft/Forge APIShared contract core across targets, with separate Minecraft and loader adaptations
DistributionOfficial API maintained in a separate repository with its own historyAPI included in the ordinary BCCE JAR; no separate SDK/API JAR is published

The observation about maps applies to genuinely exposed original holders, not every class in the old API. Likewise, do not assume every BCCE method named register follows freeze rules: the permission registry, for example, has its own behavior. The domain chapters clarify such distinctions.

Composition and Object Access

In the original model, subclasses obtain many features through a base runtime class. This is convenient when extending a particular implementation, but couples the addon to its lifecycle, fields, and state representation. Porting to another Minecraft version may require porting those dependencies as well.

In BCCE, a type describes an extension's composition, a component adds a specific behavior, and a host manages the instance. Allowed operations are exposed through an API view and context. For example, an item filter only needs to know the offered stack and eligible directions; it does not need access to the whole TilePipeHolder.

For deeper customization, BCCE provides PipeFlowDefinition and PipeBehaviourDefinition. These are public factories for custom API components, not permission to subclass old transport internals. Choose the narrowest contract that expresses your intended behavior: a connection rule, a routing component, an attachment, or a complete custom flow.

This separation comes at a cost: a type descriptor does not automatically supply missing capabilities. If a built-in machine type has only configuration components and no executable factory, copying its definition does not create a functioning new quarry. If a generic signal channel is registered but the backend handles only classic wires, a new ID will not create its own network. These limits matter when selecting an integration point.

Transfer Results Have Different Semantics

When migrating MJ code, compare return-value semantics carefully. The old IMjReceiver.receivePower(offered, simulate) returned the excess that was not accepted. BCCE's MjTransferResult.transferred() reports the accepted amount, while remainder() reports what is left.

Simply renaming a method can therefore reverse your energy accounting. Previously, the accepted amount was offered - excess; the new API exposes it directly. ExternalEnergyPort.insert returns the accepted quantity in the external system's units. Normalize these results at adapter boundaries and test zero, partial, and complete transfers.

Both systems support simulation, but BCCE also makes limitations of generic policies explicit. The default ALL_OR_NOTHING method refuses to execute without an appropriate atomic backend. This distinguishes a real port guarantee from two independent calls in sequence.

Persisted Data Is Independent of Java Class Names

In the original robot API, saved data can contain a registered AI/resource name. RobotManager then locates the corresponding Java class, instantiated through reflection by AIRobot or ResourceId. Legacy class-name fields also participate in migration. Thus the original model did have named registration, but restoration was still tied to specific classes and constructors.

In BCCE, a public persistent type describes a codec and schema version. An addon can rename its Java class while keeping the same ID and data format. If the format changes, it supplies a migration. For unknown types, a supporting host retains the raw payload instead of instantiating an arbitrary class from saved data.

These guarantees are domain-specific: check how the actual host uses aliases, migrations, and unknown state. The existence of a shared PersistentType does not prove that every domain automatically performs all these steps.

Shared API and Actual Guarantees

BCCE declares buildcraft.api.v2 as the supported namespace and exposes a contract version. This separates addon code from mod implementation details: new integrations should depend on public types rather than internal classes, client code, or loader-specific APIs.

However, an identical API version does not guarantee identical edge-case behavior on every target. Backends for different Minecraft families, including 26.X, vary in callback exception handling. A feature flag alone cannot promise full arbitrary-transport support, automatic permission checks in every method, or atomic writes across multiple worlds.

The practical benefit of this new layer is more explicit, localized dependencies. An addon depends on a clear contract for resources, state, and operations; adaptation to Minecraft and its loader remains a separate concern. Actual feature coverage depends on the hosts and consumers discussed in the domain chapters.

I. Integration Fundamentals

03Your First Integration

Adding fuel is a good starting point: the extension has a stable ID, numeric parameters, a clear consumer, and a verifiable outcome. This example assumes the addon has already registered the examplemod:biofuel fluid in Minecraft. The BCCE API assigns fuel properties to it; creating the fluid, block, and bucket still uses standard Minecraft content registration.

Adding the Dependency

Public API classes are included in the regular BCCE JAR. No separate SDK/API JAR or Maven artifact named buildcraft-api-v2-* is published. Add BCCE as a development dependency for your target Minecraft version and loader.

Add the appropriate BCCE build to your loader's development environment and declare dependencies on the modules you use. The core API requires buildcraftlib; actually using fuel in gameplay also requires buildcraftenergy. Loader module IDs differ from public API module IDs: for example, BuildCraftModules.LIB has the value buildcraft:lib. Choose the dependency syntax in mods.toml or neoforge.mods.toml according to your loader version.

Do not bundle a copy of buildcraft.api.v2 in your addon's released JAR. BCCE provides these classes at runtime. Duplicating the API can create incompatible copies of types or break runtime discovery via ServiceLoader.

Shared addon code should compile without access to internal BCCE packages. You can test this boundary with a separate source set that depends only on the public API contracts and necessary Minecraft dependencies.

Registering Fuel

The following class contains the shared part of the integration. The service is passed as a parameter, so the same code can be called by a loader adapter or an isolated test.

java
package example.bcce;

import buildcraft.api.v2.energy.MjAmount;
import buildcraft.api.v2.fuels.EnergyFluidService;
import buildcraft.api.v2.fuels.FluidSelector;
import buildcraft.api.v2.fuels.FuelProfile;
import buildcraft.api.v2.reload.DefinitionProvenance;
import java.util.Objects;
import net.minecraft.resources.ResourceLocation;

public final class BiofuelIntegration {
    private BiofuelIntegration() { }

    public static void register(EnergyFluidService fuels) {
        ResourceLocation fluidId = id("examplemod:biofuel");
        ResourceLocation profileId = id("examplemod:biofuel_combustion");

        FuelProfile profile = FuelProfile.clean(
            FluidSelector.fluid(fluidId),
            MjAmount.ofMj(4).microMj(),
            12_000
        );

        fuels.register(profileId, profile,
            new DefinitionProvenance(
                "examplemod", "code:biofuel", 0
            ));
    }

    private static ResourceLocation id(String value) {
        return Objects.requireNonNull(ResourceLocation.tryParse(value));
    }
}

These numbers illustrate game balance: 4 MJ per tick and 12,000 burn ticks per bucket. FuelProfile uses micro-MJ for power, hence MjAmount.ofMj(4).microMj(). Passing the number 4 directly would mean four millionths of an MJ per tick. Fully using this profile yields 48,000 MJ of energy per bucket. This calculation describes the profile; actual engine operation also depends on its state and mode.

The fluid ID and profile ID are intentionally different. One identifies a Minecraft resource; the other identifies a BCCE rule. Stable names matter for diagnostics, conflict resolution, and maintaining integrations. Use FluidSelector.exact to match components exactly, or FluidSelector.tag for a group of fluids.

Retrieve the service from a loader adapter as follows:

java
BiofuelIntegration.register(
    BuildCraftApi.service(BuildCraftServices.ENERGY_FLUIDS)
);

This is a call-site snippet requiring imports of BuildCraftApi and BuildCraftServices. Register once during addon initialization. For ordinary API registration on existing Forge/NeoForge targets, an appropriate point is work scheduled with enqueueWork during common setup, before BCCE freezes registries at load-complete. Register Minecraft blocks, items, and entities earlier through the loader's normal registration events. The API does not define a universal RegisterBCCEAddonEvent.

Verifying the Result

After registration, the profile should be found through EnergyFluidService.findFuel(...), while its ID and provenance should appear in the service snapshot. Merely constructing a FuelProfile says nothing about successful registration. Likewise, a successful API registration does not prove that the Minecraft fluid was created.

For a gameplay test, launch the correct target build, place the fuel in a combustion engine, and test it under load. A fluid with the right ID but unsupported components or an incorrect platform adapter may never match its profile. Check the entire chain: Minecraft resource → platform port → FluidVariant → profile → consumer.

The existence of a profile codec does not imply automatic loading of arbitrary JSON files from datapacks. This example uses the actual public register method; you can implement your own reloadable definitions through DefinitionReloadService.

I. Integration Fundamentals

04Lifecycle and Extension Registration

Registration tells BCCE which extension types exist. Execution operates on instances of those types in a particular world. Keeping these stages separate allows ID conflicts and references to be checked in advance, followed by a stable registry layout that does not change on every tick.

Obtaining the Runtime

BuildCraftApi.runtime() discovers the implementation through Java ServiceLoader and caches the result in a private holder. The API expects exactly one provider. If none is found, it returns ApiRuntime.empty() with version 0.0.0 and empty services and registries. Discovery fails if multiple providers exist or the runtime's major version differs from the facade's major version.

There is no public runtime installer. An addon must not provide its own service-provider descriptor for ApiRuntime or invoke the internal bootstrap. For tests, pass the runtime to your own code as a parameter instead of replacing the game's singleton.

If BCCE is an optional dependency, the loader must determine that the mod is present before loading an integration class that imports BCCE. An empty runtime cannot help when the API classes themselves are missing: the JVM may fail to resolve those references before the method is ever called.

Bootstrap Phases

PhaseMeaning for Integration
DISCOVERYThe runtime has been discovered; the module set is still being assembled
TYPE_REGISTRATIONPreparing extension types, codecs, and handlers
CONTENT_REGISTRATIONRegistering content and connections between types
FROZENType registries are frozen; new types and aliases are not accepted
RUNNINGOperations on game instances and reads of registered definitions
STOPPINGThe shutdown stage defined by the contract

BCCE controls phase transitions. Its runtime forbids skipping phases or moving backwards. At freeze, it first validates aliases in all ApiRegistry instances and external module dependencies; only then does it freeze registries, modules, reload types, and world-event handlers. A preflight validation error should not leave half the registries frozen.

BCCE enters FROZEN and RUNNING at load-complete, before a world has started. RUNNING therefore does not mean a Level is available or that the server has loaded the desired dimension. The enum includes STOPPING, but this does not by itself create a public addon shutdown callback.

The distinction between TYPE_REGISTRATION and CONTENT_REGISTRATION helps organize code. ApiRegistry itself enforces the freeze boundary, not a separate phase for each entry type. Do not depend on constructor ordering across modules, and do not wait until load-complete to register: BCCE is already finishing its freeze there.

Type Registries

Obtain a registry using a key from BuildCraftRegistries:

java
ApiRegistry<PipeType> pipes = runtime.requireRegistry(
    BuildCraftRegistries.PIPE_TYPES
);
pipes.register(type.id(), type, () -> "examplemod");

Here, runtime and type are previously obtained objects. This pattern is shared by many domains, but constructing PipeType and its gameplay components is explained in the pipes chapter.

Prefer the overload with RegistrationContext: its owner() is stored in RegistryEntry to explain where the entry came from. The shorter overload records an owner of unknown in the current backend. In a normal registry, owner is metadata, not automatic proof of namespace ownership. Some domain services check the namespace against the owner separately.

Duplicate IDs are forbidden even if the new value appears equivalent to the old one. Repeated register calls are not updates. This also applies when an entry ID conflicts with an alias. Do not hide duplicates with an “if ID exists, skip” check: that can silently accept another addon's extension as yours.

For reads, prefer entry(id), which returns Optional<RegistryEntry<T>>. One important exception to the API's usual conventions: get(id) returns null when the entry is absent. values() returns an immutable list of values; entries() returns an unmodifiable view of entries. Before freeze, the latter may reflect later registrations; after freeze, the set is stable. An unmodifiable collection does not make arbitrary values stored inside it immutable.

Aliases and Identity

An alias resolves an old ID to a new canonical ID. Register it before freeze using registerAlias(oldId, newId, registrationContext). The third argument is a RegistrationContext, for example () -> "examplemod". The target may be added later during the same registration stage. By freeze, the alias chain must terminate at an existing entry; cycles and missing final targets are rejected.

An ID alias and a payload migration solve different problems. The former renames a type; the latter changes the structure of its saved data. Renaming examplemod:old_filter to examplemod:filter does not automatically turn the old threshold field into a new data structure.

Do not derive stable IDs from enum ordinals, Java class names, random per-launch UUIDs, or collection iteration order. IDs are part of saved data and relationships between extensions. Use separate, meaningful IDs for distinct entities: a type, component, recipe, handler, and synchronization channel may all belong to one addon but serve different purposes.

Services and External Modules

BuildCraftServices defines typed service keys. Public ApiRuntime supports looking them up, but not installing or replacing them. A ServiceKey<T> does not create a backend on its own. Passing services into your components through constructors or parameters makes dependencies explicit and simplifies testing.

An addon that is physically loaded can declare a module via ModuleService.registerExternal. In the current backend, the ID namespace must match RegistrationContext.owner(), the version must be nonblank, and loaded must be true. Freeze checks required-module existence and dependency cycles. This declaration complements loader dependency metadata but does not replace it: it cannot load a missing JAR.

Not every method called register belongs to ApiRegistry. In particular, PermissionServiceRegistry manages its own ordered collection and does not check the shared freeze boundary in the current implementation. By contrast, registration in WorldEventService, ModuleService, and DefinitionReloadService explicitly closes. Follow each service's actual contract rather than assuming that all registries behave alike.

I. Integration Fundamentals

05Resources and Transfers Between Storages

A port describes the available operations on a resource: insertion, extraction, or both. It need not represent a separate block and does not expose loader-native storage. A single port may represent one inventory side, an allowed part of a machine, or an adapter for another mod.

Resources are divided into items, fluids, MJ, and external energy. They share the concepts of operation modes and amounts actually transferred, but use different value and result types. Do not flatten them into an untyped number with no unit or resource identity.

Simulation and Execution

OperationMode.SIMULATE checks an operation without modifying storage state. EXECUTE performs the actual operation. ItemPort and FluidPort implementations must honor this contract: simulation must not consume supplies, occupy capacity, create items, or mark storage dirty.

Simulation does not create a reservation. Free capacity, resource identity, or permissions can change between simulation and execution. The EXECUTE result is therefore authoritative and must be used for actual debiting and accounting.

For example, a port may accept 1,000 mB during simulation but only 600 mB during execution. The source must lose only the 600 mB actually transferred; the remaining 400 mB stays with the operation's owner. A successful simulation does not authorize removing an entire bucket.

SIMULATE is not a universal world transaction. It does not combine arbitrary extraction from one port with insertion into another. Higher-level services may also perform housekeeping: for example, checking request-logistics delivery can update timeouts. Read the specific operation contract rather than assuming all high-level operations follow low-level port semantics.

Items

ItemPort.insert(ItemStack, mode) returns ItemTransferResult, where transferredCount() is the accepted item count and remainderCount() is the difference between offered and accepted counts. For extraction, the result contains the actual extracted stack. transferred() returns a copy; modifying it does not alter the result.

Item counts use int. Negative requests and results exceeding the request are rejected. A zero transfer is an ordinary response from a full, incompatible, or unavailable port, not necessarily an error. completed() means the quantity request was fulfilled; for a zero request it may be true while movedAnything() == false.

ItemMatcher tests a stack. Built-in matchers any() and none() compose with and, or, and negate. examples() supplies optional representative stacks for interfaces; an empty list does not mean the matcher can never succeed. More complex rules, tags, and exact component matching are covered in the lists and recipes chapters.

When slot positions matter, a port may additionally implement SlottedItemPort, exposing slots(), stackInSlot(slot), and the effective filter(slot). The filter is an admission rule and may be more complex than a single item example. Slot access is optional: ordinary ItemPort need not expose slots. A stack returned for inspection must not be used to bypass transfer methods; the slot-view contract does not make it a mutation mechanism.

Insertion with ItemTransferPolicy.PARTIAL permits partial acceptance. The default ALL_OR_NOTHING implementation has a crucial behavior: successful simulation does not lead to execution. In EXECUTE, it conservatively transfers nothing unless the specific port overrides it with a genuine atomic guarantee. This prevents a false all-or-nothing promise on a port that supports only partial insertion.

The default extraction overload with minCount and maxCount works similarly. With a positive minimum, the generic method does not execute extraction without a special implementation. Simulating the minimum and hoping execution behaves the same is insufficient. A zero minimum permits ordinary partial extraction.

Item Ownership During Transfers

A practical way to connect two arbitrary storages is an intermediate machine-owned buffer. The machine first takes the extracted resource into its own buffer. It then offers the contents to the destination and deducts only what was actually transferred. Unaccepted items remain in the buffer and are persisted with the machine.

The following snippet assumes a buffer exclusively owned by the caller for the duration of the operation:

java
ItemStack offered = ownedBuffer.copy();
ItemTransferResult result = destination.insert(
    offered, OperationMode.EXECUTE
);
ownedBuffer.shrink(result.transferredCount());

There is no extraction from an external source in this snippet. ownedBuffer already belongs to the sender; a copy is offered, and the sender deducts according to the destination's result. The caller must prevent re-entry and concurrent modification of the buffer. If the buffer changes, its owner must also mark it dirty and persist it.

The pattern “extract everything, insert whatever fits, discard the remainder” is wrong. Re-inserting the remainder into the source is not a universal rollback either: the source may have stopped accepting it. Reliable integrations define an owner for every item at every stage.

Fluid Identity

Fluids are represented by several small concepts:

ConceptMeaning
FluidVariantFluid ID and immutable component data
FluidComponentPayloadFormat ID and canonical bytes of opaque components
FluidAmountNonnegative quantity in mB, stored as long
FluidVolumeA variant and quantity, or a special empty volume
FluidMatcherRule selecting acceptable variants
FluidTransferResultRequested quantity, transferred volume, and remainder

FluidVariant.sameFluid compares IDs only. sameVariant and equals also compare the component format and bytes. Two fluids with the same ID may be different variants. If components encode composition, temperature, or other resource properties, matching by ID alone loses that identity.

The public layer does not interpret opaque bytes as NBT or JSON. Their format belongs to the adapter or addon that produces them. FluidComponentPayload copies byte arrays both on construction and on reading. The producer must guarantee byte canonicalization: semantically identical data must serialize identically when it needs to compare as the same variant.

stableHash64() computes a stable hash from the ID, format, and bytes. It is useful for indexes and diagnostics, but cannot replace equality checks: matching hashes alone do not prove two resources are identical.

Creating FluidVariant.of(id) does not check whether a fluid exists in Minecraft. The FluidService contract provides fluid registration checks, a matcher context, and a codec, but BCCE 8.0.24 has no standard BuildCraftServices.FLUIDS key or universal backend installed for it. Use your domain's service or your own platform adapter; do not reference a nonexistent key.

Volumes, Filters, and Results

One bucket equals 1,000 mB. FluidAmount.plus and minus check overflow, and a negative result is invalid. FluidVolume.of(variant, 0) normalizes to an empty volume without a variant. Do not call requireVariant() on an empty result, and do not turn an empty volume into a nonempty one without specifying the variant.

FluidMatcher.exact matches the precise variant, fluid(id) matches all variants with an ID, and tag(id) matches tagged fluids using the supplied FluidMatchContext. Tags are resolved for each operation rather than captured as a fixed list when the matcher is constructed. Custom matchers must respect the actual context and must not modify the world.

On insertion, FluidTransferResult.ofInsertion(offered, accepted) checks that acceptance never exceeds the offer. On extraction, ofExtraction(requested, extracted) checks the upper bound. The result contains fluid actually transferred, not what remains in the source. remainderAmount() returns the numerical difference. FluidPort has no generic all-or-nothing overload.

FluidVariant.CODEC converts a variant to its FluidVariantData representation. It is a value codec, not a ready-made file loader or a converter for arbitrary loader-native FluidStack values. Conversion between the API and the loader belongs at the platform boundary.

Platform Units and Containers

FluidUnitConverter calculates an exact rational conversion between mB and a platform's units per bucket. UnitConversionResult expresses the result as whole + remainder / divisor; exact() checks whether a remainder exists. If the platform uses finer units, dropping the remainder on every transfer creates systematic resource loss. Preserve it in an owner-controlled buffer or reject inexact conversions.

PlatformServices supplies optional ItemTransfer, FluidTransfer, and EnergyTransfer adapters. Their find(level, pos, side) methods locate a port on a block side. A missing platform adapter and a missing port at a position are different reasons for an empty Optional. The direction refers to the queried or receiving block's side; when querying a neighbor, this is normally the side facing the source.

Directly locating a platform port does not automatically supply an actor or check permissions. If an operation runs on behalf of a machine and must honor permissions, use the appropriate world-access context or an explicit permission check. Nor should a block port be cached indefinitely across chunk unloads or BlockEntity replacement.

FluidItemAdapter lets you declare which fluid an item represents. FluidItemService takes the first applicable nonempty result in adapter registration order. These contracts describe contents; they do not provide a universal action for emptying buckets or capsules. Consuming the item and returning its empty container require separate logic, or the same item could yield its contents repeatedly.

I. Integration Fundamentals

06Operation Context and Permissions

Automation must identify on whose behalf it operates and what object it changes. The API uses AutomationActor, WorldOperationContext, and PermissionService for this purpose. One integration can then serve a quarry, robot, or other machine without depending on BCCE's internal FakePlayer.

Actor Identity

AutomationActor distinguishes players (PLAYER), machine owners (MACHINE_OWNER), the system (SYSTEM), and unknown owners (UNKNOWN). The first two require a player UUID. Machines and systems have a sourceId that identifies the automation source using a stable ID rather than a Java class name. ActorService provides factories for these identities.

The player name is supplemental data. An actor's equality with a UUID does not change when a player changes their name; kind, UUID, and source are considered. This is useful for validating ownership after loading saved data. OwnedView only exposes an owner's UUID for reading; it is not itself a permission store.

An actor describes the request's provenance. Constructing AutomationActor.system(...) does not grant elevated permissions, and creating machineOwner(...) does not authenticate the supplied UUID. These values must come from trusted placed-machine state or a verified player action. Some current backend domain callbacks pass unknown; such a context must not automatically be treated as the machine owner.

The Complete Permission Request

WorldOperationContext contains the actor, level and dimension, origin position, target, operation kind, mode, and optional reason ID. WorldOperationTarget may identify a block, an entity UUID, both, or neither. Choose the exact WorldOperationKind: breaking, placing, interacting, inventory access, draining fluids, and force-loading chunks have different implications for world protection.

Coordinates in this context are copied as immutable BlockPos values. However, a Level reference still points to a live world. An immutable wrapper stabilizes the request description, not the world itself; it does not make arbitrary level.setBlock calls safe.

ExtensionContext serves another purpose: it publishes explicitly available typed views through ContextKey<T>. For example, a callback can obtain PIPE, MACHINE, ITEM_PORT, or ROBOT from BuildCraftContextKeys. An empty Optional means that view is not published for this operation. Do not cast a view into an internal BlockEntity to circumvent its boundaries.

How Decisions Are Combined

PermissionService.decide(context) returns PermissionDecision with ALLOW, DENY, or PASS. Allow and deny decisions require an authority ID; a reason explains the outcome. PASS means the provider offers no decision, not explicit permission.

PermissionServiceRegistry sorts handlers by descending priority and then string ID. The first DENY stops evaluation. The first ALLOW is remembered, but later handlers may still deny the action. A high-priority allowing provider therefore cannot bypass another provider's protection. If everyone returns PASS, the aggregate remains PASS, and the calling domain applies its policy.

PermissionServices.compose combines supplied services in collection order, with the same terminal DENY rule, but does not sort them. Both forms require non-null decisions. Checks must be observational in either mode: a permission decision must not itself break a block or consume an item.

Repeat necessary checks against current state when executing. A decision obtained during preview is not a long-lived authorization. An implementation accepting an actor does not necessarily call a permission service itself, as documented for schematic placement, gate programs, and some attachment operations.

World Events

WorldEventService allows registering handlers before freeze for BLOCK_INTERACT, BEFORE_BLOCK_PLACE, BLOCK_PLACED, and PIPE_PLACED. The first two are cancellable; the latter two notify about completed actions. Returning DENY after placement does not undo the block.

Events contain typed WorldEventContext snapshots. Handlers run by priority and ID on the server thread. In the current shared implementation, cancellable events are denied when requested on the client, off the server thread, or for an unloaded position. Handler exceptions also deny cancellable events; for notifications they cannot undo already completed operations. When porting an integration, verify the selected family backend because the public contract and precise exception-isolation behavior can differ among implementations.

This is a BCCE event bus with specific invocation points, not a subscription to every vanilla or loader event. If another mod directly changes a block, merely installing WorldEventService does not intercept that change.

I. Integration Fundamentals

07State Persistence and Schema Evolution

Extension state should survive world reloads, Java class renames, and temporary absence of an addon. The API separates type identity from implementation: persisted data holds a stable ID and schema version, while a codec transforms the payload.

Three Layers of Data

PersistentType<T, P> describes a type: its ID, current schema version, ApiCodec<T, P>, aliases, and migration steps. T is an addon's runtime value, while P is its serialized representation. The public codec is not tied to NBT: concrete domains may use NBT, JSON, OpaqueData, or another supported representation.

EncodedPayload<P> is the saved envelope containing typeId, schemaVersion, and payload. PayloadResolution<T, P> resolves it to a KnownPayload with a runtime value or an UnknownPayload containing original data. Constructing a PersistentType does not register it in some universal global persistence service. A domain retrieves its persistent type through its own contract, such as a component or robot task type.

ApiCodec.decode and encode return CodecResult. Represent expected format errors with failure rather than returning null. valueOrThrow() is convenient when an error should truly abort an operation; while loading saved data, you usually need to handle successful(), errors, and unknown payloads.

Schema Versions

A schema version belongs to one persistent type. It need not match API 2.1.0, BCCE 8.0.24, or the Minecraft version. Increment it when old payloads cannot be read correctly using the new format without conversion.

SchemaMigration<P> defines a deterministic fromVersion() → toVersion() transition. The builder requires nonnegative starting versions, forward movement, no transition beyond the current schema, and at most one transition from each source version. These checks do not prove that every historical version has a path; the developer must supply the necessary migrations.

If schema 1 stored a single limit, while schema 2 stores a limit and mode, the migration must explicitly choose the new mode's value. Never silently interpret old bytes as a new structure just because the payload length happens to match. Validate numeric ranges, lengths, allowed IDs, and trailing data where relevant.

Aliases in PersistentType and a domain's ApiRegistry are not interchangeable. Whether they are used depends on the real host. For example, robot task saves use registry resolution of persistent types, whereas snapshot-element loading starts with SNAPSHOT_ELEMENT_TYPES.get(storedTypeId). To rename such an element, register the alias specifically in BuildCraftRegistries.SNAPSHOT_ELEMENT_TYPES using registerAlias(oldId, newId, registrationContext). That alias participates in the initial lookup; PersistentType.alias(...) alone is insufficient. The new type's codec must return an element with the correct current typeId().

Unknown Data

UnknownPayloadReason distinguishes missing types, newer schemas, missing migrations, migration failures, and decode failures. None of these unknown values may execute as ordinary components. Their purpose is to preserve the original data until it can be understood again.

When saving again, retain the original storedTypeId, storedSchemaVersion, and raw payload. Replacing an unknown component with an empty instance of your own type destroys the possibility of recovery. UnknownPayload.toEncodedPayload(copier) helps reconstruct an envelope with copied data.

Safe storage of generic payloads depends on copying. UnknownPayload and EncodedPayload cannot universally deep-copy an arbitrary P. PayloadCopier.immutable() is suitable only for truly immutable representations. Mutable NBT or collections require a copier that prevents shared mutable references. OpaqueData already copies its bytes on construction and access, making it useful for small component states.

This model supports data recovery but does not make every save a game-wide transaction. Coordinated changes to two worlds or BlockEntities can still be written at different times. Validate state after loading, and explicitly define what happens to incomplete operations.

Practical Implementation Order

First identify the minimal state you really need to save. Do not store Level, BlockEntity, services, callbacks, or views in the payload. Recreate them from IDs and context after loading. Then implement the codec and known migrations, attach the definition to the domain type, and verify the host's behavior.

Useful tests include a normal round trip, an older schema, an unknown ID, a newer schema, and saving again while the addon is absent. Also check that modifying a returned copy of an array or NBT value cannot change stored state. Stay within any payload-size limits enforced by the host.

I. Integration Fundamentals

08Reloadable Definitions

Extension types are normally frozen at startup, but configuration values and rules may change during execution. DefinitionReloadService defines a separate model for this: a registered data domain, incoming definitions, a validated candidate, and an atomically published snapshot.

Reload is not another ApiLifecycle phase. It can happen repeatedly after freeze. On failure, the previous snapshot remains active and the caller receives diagnostics.

Domain, Decoder, and Sources

ScriptableDefinitionType<T> specifies a domain ID, Java result type, and default decoder. Register it before freeze with an owner matching the ID's namespace. Additional named decoders are selected through the input data's string type field. If absent, the default decoder is used. If present but not registered, the definition is invalid.

Definitions are supplied as ScriptedDefinition, in three forms: VALUE, ALIAS, and DISABLED. A value has a structured map, an alias has a target ID, and a disabled record must have a reason. A record cannot be both a value and an alias.

Nested data is restricted to JSON-like values: strings, numbers, booleans, null, lists, and maps with string keys. It is defensively copied, and nesting deeper than the limit of 48 is rejected. A decoded T must also be immutable or manage its own state correctly: an immutable outer snapshot cannot freeze an arbitrary user-provided object.

ReloadContributor resupplies code-owned definitions for each attempt; its output does not accumulate across generations. DefinitionProvenance contains owner, source, and priority, explaining where a value came from and why it prevailed.

A Minimal Rules Domain

This example describes string-valued addon rules. It is a complete shared class for registering a domain; the reload itself happens separately after freeze.

java
package example.bcce;

import buildcraft.api.v2.reload.DefinitionReloadService;
import buildcraft.api.v2.reload.ScriptableDefinitionType;
import java.util.Objects;
import net.minecraft.resources.ResourceLocation;

public final class RuleDefinitions {
    public static final ScriptableDefinitionType<String> RULES =
        new ScriptableDefinitionType<>(
            Objects.requireNonNull(
                ResourceLocation.tryParse("examplemod:rules")
            ),
            String.class,
            data -> {
                Object value = data.get("value");
                if (!(value instanceof String text) || text.isBlank()) {
                    throw new IllegalArgumentException("value is required");
                }
                return text;
            }
        );

    private RuleDefinitions() { }

    public static void register(DefinitionReloadService service) {
        service.registerType(RULES, () -> "examplemod");
    }
}

After freeze, the data adapter supplies the complete input set for another reload attempt:

java
ReloadPublishResult result = service.reload(
    RuleDefinitions.RULES,
    List.of(ScriptedDefinition.value(
        Objects.requireNonNull(
            ResourceLocation.tryParse("examplemod:delivery_policy")
        ),
        Map.of("value", "prefer_existing_route"),
        new DefinitionProvenance("examplemod", "config:delivery", 10)
    ))
);

This snippet assumes an existing DefinitionReloadService service and imports from reload and java.util. The config:delivery path is source metadata, not an automatically loaded filename. Reading files, integrating with /reload, and choosing a thread are responsibilities of the calling adapter. BCCE 8.0.24 does not provide a universal JSON directory that automatically feeds arbitrary domains to this service.

Conflict Resolution

Definitions are grouped by ID. The highest-priority entry wins. If two top candidates have the same priority, it is a conflict and publication is rejected. Sorting by owner and source additionally makes diagnostics deterministic, but does not resolve equal-priority ties.

The rule applies equally to values, aliases, and disabled records. A higher-priority DISABLED can explicitly disable a value, for example. For a normal value, ResolvedDefinition records the winner and lower-priority values it superseded and successfully decoded. An error in a fully shadowed lower-priority value need not invalidate the result; an error in the winner does.

An alias may point through other aliases, but its chain must terminate at an enabled value. Cycles, missing IDs, and disabled final targets are errors. ScriptedDefinitionSnapshot.get(id) resolves aliases and respects disabled records.

Publishing and Observers

After decoding and validating references, the service creates a candidate snapshot. All ReloadObserver.beforePublish callbacks run in registration order. An exception from one rejects the candidate. Only once validation succeeds does the service replace the current domain snapshot in a single assignment. afterPublish callbacks then run; their failures are recorded as warnings and cannot roll back already published data.

This guarantee applies to one ScriptableDefinitionType domain. Two independent reload calls do not form a transaction covering all BCCE registries. The service also cannot undo arbitrary external changes made by callbacks. Thus beforePublish should validate the candidate rather than mutate the world in advance. Side effects after commit must assume the data is already published.

ReloadGeneration identifies an attempt. Failed attempts consume numbers too, so successfully published generations may have gaps. ReloadPublishResult.generation() describes the latest attempt, whereas snapshot(...).generation() describes the actually published data. Compare both with published() and diagnostics.

Do not recursively reload the same domain from its callback: the current implementation rejects recursive publication. Service synchronization protects the publishing process; it does not allow observers to access the Minecraft world from arbitrary background threads.

Interaction with Recipes and Fuel

EnergyFluidService and MachineRecipeService also provide definition snapshots but are not automatically connected to DefinitionReloadService. Their implementations contain internal data-replacement mechanisms and codecs; no public automatic JSON/datapack path to these domains is available. Add definitions through the corresponding public registration methods.

This matters for config and scripting-mod integrations: having a data format is not the same as having a loader for it. An adapter must explicitly translate incoming data into the chosen supported contract.

II. Machines and Energy

09Machines: Your Own Block and Runtime Rules

Use the machine API when your addon creates its own machine and needs to integrate with BCCE energy, pipes, gates, and monitoring tools. It is based on composition: a machine definition specifies components and settings, while a separate executable object manages component lifecycles. The addon remains the owner of the block, inventories, and world interactions.

Three objects serve three different purposes. MachineType describes a kind of machine: its stable ID, components, and properties. MachineHost represents one running machine in a world. MachineHostOwner connects the host to the addon's block entity: it supplies location and logical side, exposes ports, persists state, and sends network packets. Creating a host does not register a Minecraft block, create a block entity, menu, or model, or start an independent ticker.

This lets you use your mod's normal block entity. You do not need to subclass a BCCE Quarry, Distiller, or other implementation. The custom resource-processing algorithm must still live somewhere: it belongs in the addon's executable components.

Define the Type Before Creating an Instance

A component has a stable typeId(). To perform work each tick, it additionally implements MachineTickComponent; to report pending work, MachineWorkComponent; and to handle menu actions, MachineActionComponent. MachineComponentLifecycle adds load, activation, suspension, and removal callbacks. These interfaces can coexist on one class. They describe the component's capabilities, not separate objects that the host automatically creates for it.

MachineComponentType<C> associates an ID with a factory, optional persistence codec, and optional client-presentation codec. The MachineComponentFactory<C> receives MachineExecutionContext; a component restored from saved state receives the same context through attached. Both codec IDs must match the component ID; a mismatch is rejected when creating the type definition.

A practical integration sequence is:

  1. Define the ID, component type, factory, and necessary codecs. Register the component type before freezing registries.

  2. Build a MachineType, add the component ID, and register the resulting definition.

  3. From the block entity, once its logical side is known, create the host through BuildCraftServices.MACHINES.

  4. Connect ordinary block-entity callbacks to the host: state loading, ticking, unloading, removal, and synchronization.

  5. Implement MachineHostProvider so other BCCE systems discover this same host instance.

The following snippet connects definitions from CustomMachineFixtureAddon. Here, owner is the block entity's implementation of MachineHostOwner; registration and instance creation occur at their respective phases, not together on every tick.

java
ContentRegistrar content = BuildCraftContent.addon("fixture");
content.machineComponent(CustomMachineFixtureAddon.PRESS);
MachineType definition = content.machine(CustomMachineFixtureAddon.MACHINE);

// В block entity, после регистрации и определения логической стороны:
MachineHost host = BuildCraftApi.service(BuildCraftServices.MACHINES)
    .createHost(definition, owner);

The host checks more than the ID: in the current implementation, definition must be the exact MachineType object stored in the registry. Reconstructing an equal definition with the same ID is insufficient. Keep the registration result or retrieve it from MACHINE_TYPES.

A component without a factory is a valid descriptor, but the host does not create a running instance from it. An unknown component ID does not magically acquire default behavior either. After integration, check that host.component(id, ExpectedClass.class) returns the expected server-side object.

Machine Settings and Variants

MachineType.builder(id) assembles an immutable definition. component, removeComponent, and clearComponents manage composition; property and removeProperty manage settings. MachineType.variant(newId, base) and base.copyAs(newId) copy a definition under a new ID. copyFrom replaces the builder's current contents with the specified base.

MachineProperty<T> contains an ID, a Java type, and optionally a value validator. Properties can describe range, speed, capacity, or operating costs. Actual behavior belongs to a component that reads the property. Adding an unused property changes nothing.

The shared keys in BuiltInMachineProperties define the following common settings:

PropertyMeaning and Validation
WORK_SPEED_MULTIPLIERFinite speed multiplier strictly greater than zero.
ENERGY_COST_MULTIPLIERFinite cost multiplier greater than or equal to zero.
MAX_MJ_INPUT_PER_TICKMaximum MJ input per tick as MjAmount.
MJ_CAPACITYMJ capacity as MjAmount.
INVENTORY_SLOTSNonnegative slot count.
RANGENonnegative operating range.
CHUNK_LOADINGDescriptor-level permission to keep chunks loaded.

Two MachineProperty keys are equal by ID and Java type. Reuse the published key for common settings: creating another key with a different validator does not establish a separate namespace. Standard nested collections and arrays in definitions are copied; arbitrary mutable user values are not universally deep-copied. Prefer immutable values.

Boundary of Built-In Functionality. In BCCE 8.0.24, built-in ENERGY, MINING, PUMPING, DISTILLATION, and other machine component descriptors are registered without factories. They describe existing machine composition. You can register a Quarry variant under a new ID, but createHost does not transfer the quarry's mining algorithm. The built-in Quarry reads some properties of its own base definition through an internal bridge; that does not grant the same implementation to arbitrary new IDs.

Accordingly, machineVariant("quarry_mk2", ...) in EasyContentFixtureAddon illustrates creating a definition. To place that variant in the game and have it mine blocks, an addon must register its own block and provide executable components. A speed multiplier or the ID buildcraft:mining is not enough.

Instance Lifecycle

A host is bound to the thread on which it was created and to its owner's fixed logical side. Do not create one in an arbitrary background task. owner.level() may return null during deserialization; owner.clientSide() must still return the correct answer.

EventOwner ActionComponent Behavior
First initialization of a new server instancerestoreState(new byte[0]) or the next onLoad()The factory creates the component, then calls attached(context).
Loading a saved instancerestoreState(bytes) before the first onLoad / tickThe codec restores the component; attached(context) and restored() follow.
Entering a loaded worldonLoad()activated() prepares components for work; the host becomes active once activation finishes.
Server ticktick()The host calls onLoad if needed, then tick(context) on running components unless mode is OFF.
Chunk unloadonChunkUnloaded()Active components receive suspended().
Return after unloadonLoad()activated() runs again without recreating the object.
Actual block removaladdDrops(list), then removed(), then invalidate()Components contribute drops, receive removed(), and finally invalidated().

removed() and invalidated() are delivered at most once. Do not call addDrops as a probe: it requests real drops, not simulation. The host copies nonempty contributed stacks, but the component and owner must coordinate inventory ownership to prevent the same items being dropped twice.

During attached, restored, and activation itself, the machine is not ready for ordinary runtime mutations. In particular, markChanged and setWorkStatus require an already active server host. Use these callbacks to bind context and prepare local state; perform runtime changes after activation, usually in tick.

OFF stops MachineTickComponent execution but does not mean unloading: suspended() is a lifecycle callback, not an off-button callback. ON and LOOP are distinct MachineControlMode values passed to components; the shared host does not implement repetitive production automatically for LOOP. Components should handle context.mode() if needed.

Controls are available through MachineView.control() when the machine exposes them. Check supportedModes() before setMode(mode, operationMode). SIMULATE validates a transition without changing it; EXECUTE applies it. setEnabled is shorthand for ON / OFF, not a distinct state. A host in this model always provides controls; a monitored native machine may return an empty control().

Resources, Status, and World Interaction

The inventory, tank, and MJ buffer belong to MachineHostOwner. Its itemPort(side), fluidPort(side), mjPort(side), and externalEnergyPort(side) expose sides of those same resources. The host only makes them available to components through MachineExecutionContext. It neither persists port contents automatically nor creates a second energy reserve.

A component checks for required ports and resources, then operates under their contracts. SIMULATE can check transfer feasibility but does not jointly reserve inventory, tank, and energy. For recipes involving several storages, the addon must coordinate its own mutations or provide explicit rollback. “Simulate everything, deduct energy, insert output” is not a global transaction. CustomMachineFixtureAddon.Press demonstrates minimal port coordination and explicitly notes this limitation.

setWorkStatus(new WorkStatus(...)) publishes a human-readable machine state: IDLE, RUNNING, BLOCKED, PAUSED, or ERROR. progress is a finite number from 0 to 1. detail is a short explanation, not a log; host serialization limits it to 256 characters. After changing component counters or other state, call markChanged() to mark persistence and client presentation as dirty and notify the owner.

hasWork() asks a separate question: is unfinished work pending? A machine without energy may be BLOCKED yet still have work for a gate to detect. The host uses a pure query from any MachineWorkComponent, combining multiple answers with logical OR. Otherwise it falls back to RUNNING / BLOCKED status. On the server, an off, inactive, or removed host reports no work. On the client, it uses synchronized RUNNING / BLOCKED status when mode is not OFF; isActive() refers to server-side component execution.

blockState(pos) and isBlockLoaded(pos) do not load chunks. setBlock(pos, state) requires an active, enabled server machine and a loaded position. Additional authorization is provided by the owner's MachineWorldAccess implementation, which must enforce claims and other world restrictions. Missing world access means denial. The host does not replace the server's protection policy.

MachineAreaView extends AreaProvider with validFrom(machinePosition) to examine whether an area is suitable for a machine. It neither creates nor keeps chunks loaded.

Persistence, Menus, and Monitoring

The server stores host.saveState() as a byte array in ordinary block-entity data. The owner's inventories, fluids, and energy are saved separately alongside it. restoreState must be called before initialization; attempting to restore an already created running machine is rejected.

A component codec may support aliases and schema migrations. If its type is missing or a payload cannot be decoded, unknown data is retained for later recovery rather than silently replaced with an empty new component. If the whole host's outer format is damaged or its machine ID mismatches, the original bytes are retained, the machine enters ERROR, and execution stops. The addon must not overwrite that record with empty state.

The client receives a presentation, not the server component instance. MachineComponentPresentation<C, S> defines a snapshot S and its separate codec. Client menus read host.presentation(componentId, View.class) and workStatus(). component(...) is for the server; presentation(...) is for the client. machineComponents() is empty on clients.

Send fullSync() to new observers. Normal updates use changedSync(), where an empty array means nothing changed. The owner sends nonempty data in its own block-entity packet and calls applySync on the client. Before applying, the host verifies target ID, format, sizes, revision, and complete decoding. Stale revisions are ignored; malformed packets must not partially modify the presentation. Send a full snapshot after reconnection.

Host safety limits in BCCE 8.0.24 are 256 component records, 64 KiB per component payload, and 1,200,000 bytes per state or packet. These protect the format; they are not recommended sizes for routine UI updates.

Register menus using normal Minecraft mechanisms. The server handler passes requests to performAction(actor, actionId, payload). The host checks activity, owner.canPlayerUse(actor), and a 4,096-byte size limit before trying components in order until one handles the action. The owner denies actions by default. Components must still validate action IDs, payload structure, and the legitimacy of the state change. MachineActionComponent does not create a network channel or menu.

Other mods discover machines with MachineService.machine(level, pos). The query returns a host published by MachineHostProvider or a direct MachineView, without loading chunks. MachineService.hasWork also accounts for native endpoints of existing BCCE machines. MachineService.heat searches for a HeatPortProvider, host, or MachineView. Passing a side preserves the ability to expose different behavior on different block faces.

II. Machines and Energy

10MJ: Energy, Ports, and Conservation

MJ remains BuildCraft's own energy system. The BCCE API separates quantities, endpoint state, connection rules, and conversion to external energy. An addon can therefore connect its block through a public port without importing BCCE's internal battery or loader-specific capability tokens.

Units and Operation Results

MjAmount holds a nonnegative integer quantity of micro-MJ in a long: 1 MJ equals 1,000,000 micro-MJ. MjAmount.ofMj(4) is 4 MJ; MjAmount.ofMicro(4) is four millionths of an MJ. ofMj, plus, and multiplication-based FE conversion guard against overflow. minus forbids negative results.

Fields such as requiredMicroJoules in recipes are legacy names for that same micro-MJ unit. Passing 20 does not mean 20 MJ. For a 20 MJ cost, use MjAmount.ofMj(20).microMj().

MjTransferResult reports requested, transferred, and remainder. Its constructor enforces the equation:

requested = transferred + remainder.

completed() means that the remainder is zero. This is also true for a zero-quantity request, so it does not prove a machine performed useful work. For nonzero flow, check transferred().isZero().

MjPort.insert(offered, mode) and extract(requested, mode) can partially fulfill a request. With SIMULATE, the port must estimate the result without changing energy, limits, inventories, or other state. With EXECUTE, account for the amount actually transferred. stored / capacity and canInsert / canExtract describe a port but do not replace the result of an actual operation.

Connecting Your Block to a Network

For an ordinary addon, implementing MjPortProvider on the block entity is sufficient. mjPort(side) exposes that side's endpoint, and optional mjPortDescriptor(side) exposes its network properties. EnergyService.port checks a direct API provider first, then a machine view/host, and finally a platform bridge to native endpoints.

MjPortDescriptor contains networkId, a set of roles, and per-tick maximum flows. Roles distinguish consumers (CONSUMER), providers (PROVIDER), passive providers with a minimum request (PASSIVE_PROVIDER), connectors (CONNECTOR), pulse receivers (REDSTONE_RECEIVER), and readable state (READABLE). These are topology metadata. They may be queried on either logical side and must not simulate or execute resource transfers.

Without an explicit descriptor, the service may derive one from the public port. Standard MjStorage contributes its configured limits; for arbitrary ports with unknown stable rates, the limit is represented as Long.MAX_VALUE micro-MJ. This is not permission to accept that amount: actual port operations remain authoritative.

EnergyService.requested is a separate live demand query when MjDemandPort is supported. Call it during server operations, not during client connection discovery. Exposing a capability and actually requesting energy are different things.

Before adding a network edge, an API consumer may call canConnect(MjConnectionContext). The context contains the level, local block position, side, and two descriptors. Every registered MJ_CONNECTION_RULES rule must allow the connection, after which the platform bridge is considered. This method does not itself transfer energy. Addons implementing their own transport must additionally check role, network, and flow-limit compatibility; EngineHost.emit performs such checks for adjacent engine connections.

Standard Buffer and Tick Limits

Create standard storage through the service, not by importing an internal class:

java
EnergyService energy = BuildCraftApi.service(BuildCraftServices.ENERGY);
MjStorage buffer = energy.createStorage(
    new MjStoragePolicy(
        MjAmount.ofMj(100),     // номинальная ёмкость
        MjAmount.ofMj(100),     // физический верхний предел
        MjAmount.ofMj(8),       // приём за тик
        MjAmount.ofMj(4),       // отдача за тик
        true,                  // пассивная отдача
        false                  // обычный, не импульсный получатель
    ),
    MjAmount.ZERO
);

This snippet creates a buffer. For unrestricted ordinary storage, there is a createStorage(capacity) overload and one accepting an initial quantity. The block entity must own the buffer and call energy.tickStorage(buffer, level, pos) once per server tick when using tick limits or overcharge, preferably before its own transfers. This does not load chunks. Repeated calls for the same gameTime do not reset budgets. Without advancing to the next logical tick, already-used transfer allowances do not refresh.

Input and output limits are tracked independently and consumed only in EXECUTE. requested() considers both available space up to maximumStored and the remaining input budget. capacity() returns nominal capacity: overcharge may permit stored energy above that value.

maximumStored must be at least capacity. When it allows more than twice nominal capacity, tick reduces only the portion above 2 × capacity, losing one thirty-second of that excess per tick, rounded up. tickStorage sends POWER_LOSS_EFFECTS a PowerLossContext with the level, position, and energy actually lost. The current standard effect service draws nothing; do not assume particles or sound happen automatically.

For persistence, store buffer.snapshot().microMj() as a long alongside owner state. Restore with buffer.restore(MjStorageState.fromMicroMj(saved)). Physical energy is preserved; tick budgets begin anew. Values exceeding the current maximumStored are rejected. If capacity shrinks across versions, define a migration or explicit overflow policy.

Atomicity: What a Port Actually Promises

Simulation does not reserve capacity. A receiver can accept less than expected, or reject an operation, between preliminary checks and execution. Thus an arbitrary MjPort cannot be treated as a transactional storage system.

For MjTransferPolicy.ALL_OR_NOTHING, the default implementation first simulates full acceptance. With EXECUTE, it does not insert energy even if the simulation succeeded: without a dedicated atomic mechanism, returning no transfer is safer. A port that guarantees atomic insertion may override the overload. Standard MjStorageImpl in BCCE 8.0.24 does not. Do not use ALL_OR_NOTHING as a universal atomic insertion operation on standard buffers.

Similarly, the generic MjPort overload extract(minimum, maximum, mode) does not execute positive-minimum extraction based on simulation alone. A real “nothing or at least minimum” operation needs MjPassivePort or another suitable override. Standard MjStorage does implement this atomically: when less than the minimum is available, it changes no state.

MjStorage.refundExtracted(amount) returns energy that the buffer already extracted but the receiver did not accept. It rolls back an extraction, rather than inserting new energy or generating it. The standard implementation limits refunds to energy extracted during the current tick and to available space; it restores output budget without consuming input budget. Custom storage need not support refunds: its default implementation returns zero. Transfer code must handle that possibility.

FE Conversion and Display

EnergyService.conversion() returns the active microMjPerFe ratio. EnergyConversionStatus also reports whether automatic conversion is enabled, preference for external-energy display, and rate units. Do not hardcode a fixed MJ/FE ratio: it depends on configuration.

feToMicroMj performs exact multiplication. microMjToWholeFe rounds down to whole FE, and conversionRemainder preserves the indivisible remainder. feToMicroMjClamped saturates on overflow and is intended for capacity snapshots and display, not actual energy transfer.

automaticFeConversionEnabled describes BCCE's compatibility policy. It does not turn every long field, machine, or custom port into a converter. External energy uses separate public platform ports, and conversion must go through the appropriate adapter while retaining remainders.

MJ_FORMATTER supports consistent output: formatNumber returns a number, formatAmount includes MJ, and formatRate shows MJ/t or MJ/s according to the explicit EnergyRateUnit. Currently, per-second rates multiply by 20 and the formatter always displays MJ regardless of the FE display flag. If your UI must respect the user's FE preference, inspect status() and implement the corresponding display yourself.
