III. Transport and Logistics

22Item Lists and Specialized Matching Rules

The API supports three independent item-list extension mechanisms: a named filter, an item that contains its own filter, and custom matching semantics for an individual list entry. Choose based on where configuration is stored and who needs it.

Named Definitions

ItemList contains an immutable list of ItemListEntry records, each pairing an ItemMatcher with an enabled flag. ListMatchMode controls evaluation: ANY requires at least one enabled match, ALL requires all enabled entries to match, and NONE requires none to match. With no enabled entries, ANY is false, while ALL and NONE are true. This is important when editing filters: disabling all entries does not always reject all items.

Register named definitions in NAMED_ITEM_LISTS before freeze. ItemListService.register(id, definition) performs that registration; it is not a way to rewrite registries dynamically during game ticks. list(id), ids(), and matches(id, stack) read or evaluate definitions. Unknown IDs produce an empty Optional or false, not an allow-all filter.

Named lists suit shared addon policies, such as materials accepted by several machines. They do not store quantities or reserve matching items. A definition containing ItemMatcher functions also does not become arbitrarily serializable merely because it has an ID.

Items Containing Their Own Filter Configuration

ItemListAdapter checks whether an ItemStack contains a supported list (supports) and whether a target stack matches it (matches). The current ItemListServiceImpl finds such an adapter directly on listStack.getItem() when that item implements the interface. It does not iterate a separate registry of stack-backed list adapters.

This allows custom filter items to interact with BCCE list consumers without subclassing internal ItemList_BC8. The item owns the configuration, so matching must read listStack without modifying it. ItemListService.isList(stack) and matches(listStack, target) use this path, unlike the overloads accepting a namespaced ID.

Extending Entry Matching Semantics

To make a custom item participate in BCCE's existing list modes, implement ListMatchAdapter registered in LIST_MATCH_ADAPTERS. It receives ListMatchContext containing ListMatchType (TYPE, MATERIAL, CLASS), copies of source/target, and a precise flag. supports specifies which comparisons it handles; matches determines the result. An integration could, for example, match tools by its own categories or fluid containers by contents without coupling consumers to concrete item classes.

Current ListHandler OR-combines applicable adapters: any successful match is enough. An adapter that does not apply must return false from supports, rather than claiming everything and returning false from matches. For TYPE, when no adapter handles a comparison, there is a fallback for the same item without exact variant matching; falsely universal supports can disable that fallback.

examples(context) returns Optional<List<ItemStack>>. Optional.empty() asks the runtime to find examples by enumerating candidates and calling matches, whereas Optional.of(emptyList()) explicitly supplies no examples. Accurate examples can reduce expensive UI work for specialized rules. precise is an input to each adapter's semantics, not an automatic universal exactness mode for every custom comparison.

III. Transport and Logistics

23Request Logistics: Demand, Promises, and Confirmed Delivery

The Request API lets blocks and docking stations advertise item demand and accept deliveries. Its advanced form tracks promised and received amounts persistently. It does not plan routes, choose robots, or create a second inventory: those responsibilities remain with robot runtime or addon logistics.

Simple Request Providers

ItemRequest describes a stable ID, matcher, minimum, maximum, and priority. Counts refer to items: minimum is nonnegative and maximum must be at least minimum. RequestProvider.requests() reports current requests; offer(requestId, stack, mode) tries to accept an item for one and returns an actual ItemTransferResult.

Stable IDs avoid relying on slot indexes. Consumers must not assume the first entry always represents the same request: the order and set may change. Providers are responsible for reducing demand after real insertion, correctly implementing SIMULATE, and matching the actual request criteria.

RequestService.provider(level, pos, side) finds a provider on a loaded block entity or docking station. The current providers(level) enumerates providers at registered robot docks, deduplicating objects. It does not scan every block entity in the world or maintain a complete index of addon requesters.

For discovery by classic delivery robots, a matcher must provide at least one truly matching ItemStack through ItemMatcher.examples(). A predicate that correctly implements matches but supplies no examples may be insufficient for that integration path.

When You Need RequestLedger

ManagedRequestProvider combines a provider with RequestLedger, requestTime(), and insertRequested(requestId, offered, mode). The last method only performs real insertion into an inventory/port and reports actual acceptance; it must not update the ledger itself. The ledger accounts for each successful result once.

RequestLedger is created on its owner's thread and enforces that affinity for every operation, including saving. For a block entity, this is the server thread. Its constructor callback should only mark the host dirty, not recursively mutate the ledger. Open individual requests with open(definition, owner, now, durationTicks).

Once opened, the ledger tracks three quantities: confirmed accepted items, actively promised items, and items still available for promises. RequestLedger.RequestView shows request state, PromiseView shows one promise, and snapshots() returns current request views. For each request snapshot:

available = max(0, maximum − confirmed − reserved).

outstanding = max(0, maximum − confirmed) includes quantities already promised to other couriers. available prevents assigning the same demand to multiple senders. requests() exposes only open matcher-bound requests with positive availability, sorted by descending priority and then ID.

In the current ledger, reaching minimum does not complete a request: COMPLETE occurs when confirmed == maximum. The minimum remains part of the demand descriptor. For a requirement of “exactly 32 items,” use minimum = maximum = 32, as in the fixture.

Calling open again with the same ID, compatible numeric parameters, and the same owner rebinds the definition; it does not create a new batch or extend the deadline. Do not reuse a completed ID to start a new delivery. After reconciliation, remove the old request using forget and assign a new stable ID for the next batch.

Reserving a Promise

reserve(requestId, token, count, actor, now, durationTicks) creates a promise for a particular courier. The token is a UUID kept by the sender. Despite “up to” wording in a short comment, the implementation requires the entire count to fit within available; otherwise it returns an empty Optional. It does not reduce requested reservations automatically.

Reusing a token is idempotent only for the same request ID, actor, and count. Inconsistent reuse causes an error. A reservation deadline cannot exceed its parent request's deadline. Duration zero means no ordinary expiry; times are game ticks, not system milliseconds.

release(token, actor) frees the unfulfilled remainder and may be invoked by the courier or request owner. cancel(requestId, owner, reason) closes demand and active promises and is limited to the creator. Request states are OPEN, COMPLETE, CANCELLED, TIMED_OUT; promise states are ACTIVE, COMPLETE, RELEASED, CANCELLED, TIMED_OUT.

For remote loaded providers, the RequestService.reserve/cancel/deliver facade additionally checks inventory-access permissions. Direct ledger calls enforce internal owner/courier identity but do not replace world-access policy.

Executing Deliveries and Preventing Duplicates

Delivery uses two different UUIDs: a reservation token binds a promise, while a delivery ID identifies one insertion attempt. RequestLedger.deliver limits the offered stack to the promise remainder, checks actor, matcher, deadlines, and phase, then calls insertRequested.

DeliveryResult deliberately distinguishes accepted from acknowledged:

StatusacceptedacknowledgedMeaning
MOVED / PARTIALNew quantity actually inserted0The sender deducts only accepted
SIMULATED0Potential acceptanceDeduct nothing
DUPLICATE0Previously acknowledged quantityThe provider was not called again; nothing is deducted twice
Other rejection0Usually 0Inspect status and diagnostics

The remaining field in a calculated delivery result refers to that particular offer, not the entire request. Some early RequestService failures are constructed without the offered count and return zero here. Do not treat it as an instruction to delete or replace the source stack after an error. Use request/promise snapshots for remaining demand and only new accepted quantities for deductions. BLOCKED can mean a mismatched item, full destination, or ledger limits; UNAVAILABLE can mean unknown/unbound promises or requesters; DENIED, EXPIRED, CLOSED, and FAILED refine the failure cause.

This snippet shows a sender that already owns a stack, a reservationId, and a unique deliveryId. requests refers to RequestService. It demonstrates handling a result, not a complete universal extraction transaction.

java
RequestLedger.DeliveryResult result = requests.deliver(
    level, origin, destination, side,
    reservationId, deliveryId, offered,
    actor, OperationMode.EXECUTE);

if (result.status() == RequestLedger.DeliveryStatus.MOVED
        || result.status() == RequestLedger.DeliveryStatus.PARTIAL) {
    int newlyDelivered = result.accepted();
    // Зафиксировать расход только newlyDelivered в собственном
    // протоколе владения отправленным стеком.
}

A real sender must define when the item moves out of its inventory into transit. Do not repeatedly submit a copy of the same item under new delivery IDs. Use the previous delivery ID when retrying acknowledgement of an already performed attempt, or a new ID for an actual new insertion of the remainder. LogisticsPipesParityAddon illustrates managed-provider and routing-payload structures, but its stock counter is a fixture, not a production inventory.

If a provider throws after possibly inserting items or returns an invalid transfer result during EXECUTE, the ledger closes the indeterminate request and its promises. This prevents blindly repeating unknown outcomes forever; it does not roll back an external inventory that may already have changed. Senders need a reconciliation path, not an automatic retry using a new ID.

Persistence, Timeouts, and Guarantee Limits

Hosts must save ledger.save() alongside inventory and restore it before opening requests. Matchers are not serialized: after loading, the addon rebinds definitions through open using the same stable IDs and numeric parameters. Unbound requests and promises are retained, but do not serve new deliveries.

load(bytes) rejects corrupt or unrecognized formats without replacing current state with partially decoded data. loadPreserving(bytes) retains a bounded unsupported payload unchanged and forbids further writes until successfully decoded. This preserves incompatible data; it does not justify silently starting a fresh empty ledger.

advance(now) moves server game time forward monotonically and closes expired records. Hosts must call it with current world time, including after chunk load. Default ManagedRequestProvider methods and the delivery path also call it. Thus SIMULATE delivery does not insert items but may still update timeout accounting. Do not promise that every SIMULATE call leaves all ledger fields byte-for-byte unchanged.

The current ledger is limited to 1 MiB, 512 requests, 2,048 promises, and 4,096 delivery receipts. When the receipt window fills, old acknowledgements are removed; deleting old terminal promises also removes associated receipts. Duplicate prevention holds within this bounded window, not for every UUID forever. Use forget after the owner reconciles possible outstanding deliveries.

The ledger supplies persistent local accounting but does not make two worlds' inventory saves transactional. Crash-resilient logistics require a separate protocol for parcel ownership, shipment commit, and acknowledgement reconciliation. These limits matter especially for teleporting pipes and LogisticsPipes-style addons.

IV. World, Robots, and Presentation

24Areas, Maps, and World Access

BCCE separates geometry from world interaction. An area defines where work should happen; an access context defines what can be read or obtained at that location; an actor-bound operation determines what changes are allowed. The same geometry can therefore serve a robot, machine, construction template, and map without passing BuildCraft internals between them.

Choosing Appropriate Geometry

BlockBox defines a rectangular volume in block coordinates, including both boundaries. Its constructor normalizes the corners, taking the smaller coordinate as minimum on each axis. A box from (0, 0, 0) to (1, 1, 1) therefore contains eight blocks. contains(BlockPos) tests membership, while volume() returns long and detects arithmetic overflow through Math.multiplyExact.

Zone supports arbitrary shapes. Its only required method is boolean contains(BlockPos pos). By default, bounds() is empty, meaning no known bounding box—not an empty zone. Enumerating such a zone requires your own search limits or traversal budget.

Path exposes an ordered set of points through List<BlockPos> points(). It has no pathfinding, movement speed, obstacle handling, or interpolation. empty() only checks the list. Custom implementations should return stable lists and immutable coordinates, because the interface does not copy implementation data.

AreaProvider combines optional box(), zone(), and path() views. Having a box does not imply having a path. Implementing this interface also does not guarantee every native machine discovers your block: BCCE 8.0.24 retains internal discovery points for classic area providers. Custom consumers should use AreaProvider and connect it to their own host/context as needed. Machines also expose the related public MachineAreaView contract, described in the machines chapter.

java
BlockBox bounds = new BlockBox(
    new BlockPos(10, 64, 10),
    new BlockPos(14, 66, 14)
);

Zone shell = new Zone() {
    @Override public boolean contains(BlockPos pos) {
        if (!bounds.contains(pos)) return false;
        return pos.getX() == bounds.min().getX()
            || pos.getX() == bounds.max().getX()
            || pos.getY() == bounds.min().getY()
            || pos.getY() == bounds.max().getY()
            || pos.getZ() == bounds.min().getZ()
            || pos.getZ() == bounds.max().getZ();
    }

    @Override public Optional<BlockBox> bounds() {
        return Optional.of(bounds);
    }
};

In this model, contains receives world coordinates. If the shape algorithm uses local coordinates, explicitly subtract bounds.min(). Mixing these coordinate systems is especially noticeable in Filler: the mask works near world origin but shifts incorrectly when moved.

Reading the World Through a Restricted Context

WorldAccessService.open(Level, BlockPos origin, AutomationActor) creates a world view tied to an origin and actor. scoped(Level, BlockPos, AutomationActor, BooleanSupplier valid) adds a lifetime condition. The resulting WorldAccessContext neither exposes Level nor provides direct methods for modifying blocks.

It provides world time, server-side status, loaded-position checks, block state, pipe ID and connections, and item, fluid, and external-energy ports. Pipe metadata are not mutable pipe components. The context deliberately returns Optional.empty() for absent objects, unloaded chunks, or invalid access; an empty result alone does not identify which condition occurred.

The current implementation runs operations only on the server thread, never loads chunks, and rechecks the context's validity when previously obtained ports are used. Once valid becomes false, storing the port in a field will not make later access work. Expired or otherwise invalid contexts return -1 from gameTime(), deny permission checks, and perform no transfers.

java
WorldAccessContext world = BuildCraftApi
    .service(BuildCraftServices.WORLD_ACCESS)
    .open(level, machinePos, actor);

BlockPos target = machinePos.relative(Direction.EAST);
Optional<BlockState> state = world.blockState(target);
Optional<ItemPort> input = world.itemPort(target, Direction.WEST);

Block-state reads are restricted by lifetime, thread, and chunk availability. Permission checks apply to permission(...) and port operations. Item and external-energy ports use INVENTORY_ACCESS; fluid ports use FLUID_PLACE for insertion and FLUID_DRAIN for extraction. This is not general world sandboxing: code separately given a Level still retains normal Java and Minecraft capabilities.

Do not make a callback-scoped context long-lived by wrapping it with your own () -> true predicate. Store positions and IDs, and obtain a fresh context on the next permitted call. Even successful simulation does not lock a neighbor's contents until the next tick.

Distinguishing Properties from Permissions

WorldPropertyService holds named WorldProperty predicates, useful for rules such as “this block counts as my ore” or “this position is suitable for work.” It provides register, get, properties, and test; unknown IDs test false. It does not build a cache, scan for matching blocks, or grant permission. If a predicate caches results, its owner must invalidate them. The mere existence of WorldProperty.clear() does not prove automatic cache management on every runtime path.

WorldRuleService answers other questions through isSoft, isReplaceable, mayBreak, and mayPlace. A soft block is not necessarily authorized for breaking, and allowed placement does not mean construction resources have been reserved. mayBreak and mayPlace are checks; actual changes should go through an appropriate actor-bound automation mechanism. On the server, mayPlace also simulates the pre-placement event.

25Schematics: Capturing State and Building

A schematic must preserve a block's meaning, resource requirements, and restoration method. For addons, this means more than serializing NBT: distinguish configuration from actual items and fluids, define rotation behavior, and ensure objects can recover after an addon is temporarily removed.

BCCE's public model centers on a snapshot element and a behavior adapter. SnapshotElement holds addon-owned data and returns typeId(). SnapshotElementType<E> associates the ID with PersistentType<E, OpaqueData>. A SchematicAdapter tells Builder how to capture, evaluate, and place a block. Entities have a separate EntitySchematicAdapter.

Connecting a Block to Architect and Builder

An integration has four parts:

  1. Create a snapshot element containing the minimal data needed to restore the object.

  2. Define its codec and persistence schema through PersistentType.

  3. Implement an adapter that recognizes both your block and your saved elements.

  4. Register the type and adapter before content registration closes.

ContentRegistrar.blockSchematic(String path, SnapshotElementType<E> type, SchematicAdapter adapter) registers both. The type ID must match registrar.id(path) and its persistence ID. You may register with separate snapshotElement(...) and schematicAdapter(...) calls if your architecture needs it, but must not register the type twice.

java
ContentRegistrar bc = BuildCraftContent.addon("example");
bc.blockSchematic("relay_snapshot", relaySnapshotType, relayAdapter);

Here relaySnapshotType and relayAdapter are addon-created instances of the corresponding public types. SchematicFixtureAddon shows a full PersistentType definition and joint registration; its example placement body returns success without changing the world. Do not copy that stub into a production addon as a working builder implementation.

During capture, the runtime processes adapters by descending priority(), then registration ID. supports(SchematicCaptureContext) identifies which blocks an adapter handles. capture(...) returns an element or an empty result to continue searching. The returned type must be registered. If no custom adapter applies, the current implementation falls back to BuildCraft's native snapshot handling.

Capture context contains level, snapshot origin, current position, state, and actor. Do not store the context or world object in the snapshot element. Use position - origin for relative location; a type ID and state data suffice to identify the element.

supportsElement(SnapshotElement) determines ownership of a saved element and defaults to false. An adapter implementing only supports(context) may capture blocks but then fail to be found during blueprint placement. Usually check both type ID and the expected Java class. Avoid “any non-air block” predicates in production; they steal other mods' machines and lose their special behavior.

Describing Resources and Build Order

A minimal adapter compiles with capture and place, but an inventory-bearing machine needs more. Builder asks several distinct questions that must describe one consistent operation.

Adapter ContractPurpose
requirements(element, level)Full requirements for display and resource calculation.
placementRequirements(element, level)Resources for initially placing the housing; defaults to full requirements.
requiredFluids(element, level)Fluids required for construction; defaults to requirements().fluids().
deferredItems(element, level)Items inserted after the block appears.
missingDeferredItems(element, level, position)Items still missing from an already placed block.
insertDeferredItem(..., stack, mode)Inserts a deferred item and returns its unaccepted remainder.
requiredBlockOffsets(element)Dependencies on adjacent blocks in relative coordinates.
canPlace(element, context)Whether placement at the specified position is allowed.
readyToPlace(element, context)Whether dependencies are ready for placement now.
isPlaced(element, level, position)Whether the world matches the expected result.

SchematicRequirements stores lists of items and FluidVolume values; items are copied on construction and reading. Empty requirements mean no cost, so do not leave them as the default for an expensive machine assuming Builder will discover the recipe itself.

Imagine a cabinet consisting of a housing and three installed modules. Initial requirements should include the housing, while modules can be deferred. missingDeferredItems must account for modules already installed. Otherwise, retrying after a load may request them twice or treat an unfinished cabinet as complete. In SIMULATE, insertDeferredItem computes a remainder without modifying inventory; in execution it returns the actual remainder.

rotate(element, Rotation) and requiredBlockOffsets must transform orientations and dependencies consistently. Returning the original element is correct only for state truly independent of direction. isAir defines the role of an empty element in a plan. The default placeUnchecked calls place; “Unchecked” does not absolve the addon of validating world changes.

Placing an Element and Handling Results

SchematicService offers three public operations: capture a block, capture an entity, and place one element. place(SnapshotElement, SchematicPlacementContext) receives snapshot origin, position, actor, and OperationMode. It returns SchematicResult with PASS, SUCCESS, MISSING_RESOURCE, DENIED, or FAILED and diagnostic detail.

Status must reflect the real operation. SUCCESS during simulation means the handler believes placement is feasible without performing it. PASS is not successful construction. The bridge to existing Builder treats only SUCCESS as success.

A key limitation: directly calling SchematicService.place does not consume requirements, run the full canPlace → readyToPlace → place sequence, or create a transaction. For custom elements, it locates and invokes the adapter's place. Ordinary Builder manages its own planning and supply cycle, but an external caller must implement those steps itself. Likewise, an actor in context does not mean any arbitrary level.setBlock call automatically checks permissions.

Public automation can be called inside place. This snippet maps results, with desiredState obtained from validated snapshot data. Confirm support for the relevant automation action separately.

java
AutomationResult action = BuildCraftApi
    .service(BuildCraftServices.AUTOMATION)
    .execute(new PlaceBlockRequest(
        context.level(), context.origin(), context.position(),
        desiredState, context.actor(), context.mode()
    ));

SchematicResult.Status status = switch (action.status()) {
    case SUCCESS -> SchematicResult.Status.SUCCESS;
    case DENIED -> SchematicResult.Status.DENIED;
    case PASS -> SchematicResult.Status.PASS;
    case RETRY, FAILED -> SchematicResult.Status.FAILED;
};
return new SchematicResult(status, action.detail());

This snippet does not replace resource checks, block-entity handling, or a custom isPlaced test. Builder predicate contexts may also use an unknown actor: Api2SchematicBlock creates one when no player was provided. Therefore enforce permission at execution rather than reusing a preview decision.

Preserving Contents Without Duplication

InventoryCopyPolicy exists for hidden item lists not exposed through normal platform storage. A policy contains an ID, a set of blocks, and allowed/denied DataPath values. An empty block set means it applies globally. Explicitly restrict addon policies to your own blocks whenever possible.

java
bc.inventoryCopyPolicy(InventoryCopyPolicy
    .forBlock(bc.id("relay_inventory"), bc.id("relay"))
    .allow("Items")
    .deny("InternalBuffer", "TransientItems")
    .build());

DataPath.of("InternalBuffer", "TransientItems") defines a sequence of keys, not a dotted string or a universal JSONPath language. Empty and whitespace-only segments are invalid. API policies match exact paths, and deny takes precedence over allow among applicable policies. Builder also has its own configuration rules; API policies do not automatically override them.

The native mechanism separates item contents from a block's housing NBT: known inventories are removed from restore data and their items transferred later. Otherwise Builder could place a filled container from NBT and then insert the same items again through resource requirements. A custom SchematicAdapter storing opaque payload must independently follow the same principle; registering a policy does not validate an arbitrary snapshot format.

Entities, Unknown Elements, and Model Boundaries

EntitySchematicAdapter receives SchematicEntityCaptureContext(Level, origin, entity, actor). It defines priority, matching, capture, and placement, but supplies relative position, resource requirements, and rotation rather than block dependencies. Do not interpret an entity UUID as an instruction to resurrect that same world object: the element should describe a new entity and permitted data. Requirements and codecs must preserve inventories and equipment without spawning free items.

If an element type is absent, the schema is newer than supported, or migration fails, persistence retains UnknownSnapshotElement(typeId, schemaVersion, payload), preserving original bytes for later recovery. The built-in wrapper for an unavailable block skips its position without modifying the world: it reports isPlaced/isBuilt == true to the scheduler but refuses actual placement. This is protective skipping of unknown content, not confirmation that the required block exists. Saved data remains available if the addon returns.

BlueprintMetadata(name, author, bounds) and SnapshotKind.TEMPLATE/BLUEPRINT provide metadata and snapshot-kind types, but not a universal complete blueprint object. The current API has no public builder that produces an arbitrary full blueprint in one call from those two objects. Use schematic services for elements and the separate library contracts for document formats.

26Templates, Filler, and the Electronic Library

A construction template stores shape; a blueprint stores specific contents. This gives two extension points: selecting the item that fills a template location, and defining the positions included in a Filler mask. File import/export is a separate concern: exchanging documents between tools and the player's local electronic library.

Placing Addon Items Through Templates

TemplateHandler defines boolean handle(Level level, BlockPos pos, Player actor, ItemStack stack) and optional acceptsItem(ItemStack). Register handlers with TemplateService.register(id, priority, handler); they run by descending priority, then ID. The first true stops processing.

acceptsItem matters for non-BlockItem items: without a positive result, native Builder will not select the item as template material from inventory. handle must still recheck that the item applies to it. The dispatcher does not promise to call only the same handler whose predicate originally matched the item.

In the native Builder path, it first selects and reserves one item, checks placement permission, and obtains an automation player. Only then does it call handle. Do not predicate behavior on stacks of three or five items: TemplatePlacementFixtureAddon uses a stack size of three as a test marker, but a real template step passes one reserved item. Check IDs and required components.

TemplateHandler has no OperationMode. Its handle is an executing callback; acceptsItem is an observational test. Do not invoke handle for previews. If it returns false or throws, the service can try another handler, so it must not modify the world before declining. Native Builder returns the reserved material after a failed task, but does not automatically roll back arbitrary world side effects.

Adding a Filler Pattern

FillerPattern converts FillerPatternContext into FillerMask. The context contains the box, facing, and a map of named string options. The mask exposes bounds() and tests world positions through includes(BlockPos).

java
ResourceLocation id = bc.id("checker_floor");
bc.fillerPattern(new FillerPatternType(id, context -> {
    BlockBox box = context.bounds();
    return new FillerMask() {
        @Override public BlockBox bounds() { return box; }

        @Override public boolean includes(BlockPos pos) {
            if (!box.contains(pos) || pos.getY() != box.min().getY()) {
                return false;
            }
            int x = pos.getX() - box.min().getX();
            int z = pos.getZ() - box.min().getZ();
            return ((x + z) & 1) == 0;
        }
    };
}, false));

The final FillerPatternType argument, internalOnly, hides the type from normal user selection in the Filler bridge when true, while retaining registration for programmatic consumers. FillerPatternService.type(id) and types() look up registered patterns.

The working bridge does apply addon masks through the existing Filler executor. However, the current standard wrapper calls the mask with Direction.NORTH and empty options, reports zero parameters, and provides no custom rotation. These context fields are not a promise of a complete pattern-parameter editor. External parameterized tools may call createMask with their own values; the native UI exposes only what it actually passes.

The mask is checked for every position in the volume. Do not scan the whole world inside includes, rebuild a large graph per call, or load chunks. Precompute geometry once in createMask and make membership tests cheap and deterministic.

Defining an Electronic Library Format

LibraryFormatHandler converts bytes of an external format to/from a snapshot document's CompoundTag:

java
CompoundTag decode(byte[] bytes) throws IOException;
byte[] encode(CompoundTag snapshot) throws IOException;

Register using LibraryService.register(id, extension, priority, handler). Extensions exclude the dot, are lowercase, and follow [a-z0-9][a-z0-9_-]{0,15}. bcnbt is reserved. The runtime rejects duplicate IDs or file extensions. formatForFilename chooses by filename suffix case-insensitively.

java
LibraryService library = BuildCraftApi.service(BuildCraftServices.LIBRARY);
library.register(
    bc.id("portable_blueprint"), "xblueprint", 100, portableFormat
);

Optional<CompoundTag> document = library.decode(filename, bytes);

Here, portableFormat implements LibraryFormatHandler. decode returns an empty result for an unknown extension and throws IOException for malformed content in a known format. encode(formatId, document) requires a registered ID. The service supplies defensive copies of documents and arrays and limits encoded data to 8 MiB in the current runtime. These safeguards do not establish trust: validate lengths, required fields, and format structure yourself.

An electronic-library document contains serialized BuildCraft blueprint state. Arbitrary custom NBT fields alone are insufficient for import. BlueprintLibraryFixtureAddon demonstrates conversion and validation of BLUEPRINT / TEMPLATE but does not implement full conversion of every blueprint field.

Distinguish File Conversion from Import

decode and encode only convert representations. importClient(filename, bytes) also validates the document, computes its content identity, and stores it in the local electronic library. clientEntries() returns LibraryEntry(contentId, name, kind), clientDocument(contentId) returns a document copy, and exportClient(contentId, formatId) returns encoded bytes.

These methods operate on the player's local library, not on the server world's storage. Importing a document does not put a blueprint into inventory, build anything, or bypass server-side blueprint upload rules. contentId identifies content within the library, rather than the filename. Editing a document may change its content identity.

Before importing, show the user the name, format, and expected scope of the operation. A custom integration needs access to the client environment and its local data; the mere availability of a Java interface on a dedicated server does not supply that environment.

IV. World, Robots, and Presentation

27Robots: Programs, Tasks, and Work Reservations

Robotics extensions begin with a task. An addon describes a small, persistent operation, and BCCE connects it to an existing robot executor. Access goes through RobotHandle and RobotControl; extending the internal AIRobot is unnecessary.

Keep three identities separate: a task type defines its format and behavior, a board type identifies tasks available on that board, and a board program connects the board to the Programming Table and a task factory. Registering a board descriptor alone does not create this whole chain.

Finding and Commanding a Robot

RobotService.robot(Level, long id) looks up a loaded robot. robots(Level) returns loaded instances, ordered by ID in the current implementation. Neither call loads an absent entity, and the service is not a search across every robot recorded in world saves.

RobotHandle provides an ID, optional owner, position, summary RobotStatus, current task type, and optional RobotControl. Do not serialize the handle itself; store its ID and look the robot up again. RobotStatus is an operational summary: the enum contains CHARGING, but the standard BCCE 8.0.24 implementation mainly returns ERROR, DOCKED, TRAVELLING, IDLE, and WORKING. Do not make your logic depend on every enum value being emitted.

RobotControl provides moveTo(target, mode), assign(task, mode), cancelTask(mode), and taskPhase(). In SIMULATE, assignment checks whether a persistent task can be accepted; it does not run the task or simulate the eventual route. Ordinary assignment must run on the server. Your command interface must verify that the player may control the chosen robot: these methods do not receive a separate identity for the player issuing the command.

In the current runtime, moveTo installs a separate navigation AI as the primary task. It is a robot-control command, not a guaranteed substep of the current tick. If you invoke it from your own task, account for replacement of the current executor; do not call it on every tick and expect the task stack to remain unchanged.

Implementing a Persistent Task

RobotTask requires two methods: ResourceLocation typeId() and RobotTaskResult tick(RobotTaskContext context). Results are RUNNING, COMPLETE, RETRY, or FAILED. Keep task state small and explicitly persistent: a work stage, target position, request ID, or progress counter.

java
final class InspectTask implements RobotTask {
    static final ResourceLocation ID =
        ResourceLocation.tryParse("example:inspect_area");
    private int progress;

    InspectTask(int progress) { this.progress = progress; }

    @Override public ResourceLocation typeId() { return ID; }

    @Override public RobotTaskResult tick(RobotTaskContext context) {
        // Здесь выполняется один ограниченный шаг вашей проверки.
        progress++;
        return progress >= 3
            ? RobotTaskResult.complete()
            : RobotTaskResult.running();
    }
}

This is a tick-driven state machine, not a ready-made world-scanning task. Do not scan thousands of blocks in one tick; retain the continuation in task fields. RobotTaskContext supplies the world, handle, owner's AutomationActor, and public methods for robotics reservations and requests.

For a task to be assignable, register RobotTaskType<T>(id, taskClass, persistence) through ContentRegistrar.robotTask. Its id must match the PersistentType ID. At assignment, the runtime checks the instance's Java type and whether it can be encoded. Simply implementing RobotTask without a correctly registered codec is insufficient.

RobotTaskConformanceAddon provides a complete verifiable example: progress is stored in four bytes, the format has its own ID, and the decoder validates length and range. Such checks matter: saved data must not become a negative index, an enormous loop, or an immediate resource payout.

In the current executor, RETRY keeps the task active just like RUNNING. It does not schedule a delay automatically. If you need to retry in 20 ticks, store a counter or next eligible tick in the task. FAILED ends the task unsuccessfully; an exception from tick also fails it.

Connecting a Board to In-Game Programming

java
ResourceLocation boardId = bc.id("inspection_board");

bc.robotTask(inspectTaskType);
bc.robotBoard(new RobotBoardType(
    boardId, 2, Set.of(InspectTask.ID)
));
bc.robotBoardProgram(new RobotBoardProgram(
    boardId,
    3_200,
    "blue",
    bc.id("textures/entity/inspection_robot.png"),
    robot -> new InspectTask(0)
));

inspectTaskType is a previously created RobotTaskType<InspectTask>; the shown fragment registers it once. If the type was already registered earlier in your integration, do not call bc.robotTask(inspectTaskType) again: that would cause an ID conflict. A board type contains a nonnegative tier and a set of permitted task types. RobotBoardProgram holds a positive programming cost in MJ, color, robot texture, and a Function<RobotHandle, ? extends RobotTask> factory.

Allowed colors are fixed: clean, green, blue, red, and yellow. The program ID must match the board type. The current bridge skips programs without a board type or with no tasks; when creating work, it verifies that the factory returned an allowed, persistent task type. A factory failure does not assign new work; the runtime retries later.

BuildCraftRobotBoards provides stable IDs for built-in boards, including carrier, miner, lumberjack, builder, and other types. This allows references to known content, but does not mean every internal AI task on a classic board is exposed as a registrable RobotTaskType. Define an explicit board-to-task connection for your custom program.

Handling Suspension and Recovery

RobotTaskLifecycle offers optional callbacks: onAssigned, onResumed, onSuspended, onCompleted, onFailed, and onCancelled. Phases are QUEUED, ASSIGNED, RUNNING, SUSPENDED, COMPLETED, FAILED, and CANCELLED. A terminal callback runs no more than once per task instance.

When a robot unloads, its task is suspended and runtime reservations are released. Persisted data retains the task and descriptors of required reservations. Upon recovery, those reservations must first be reacquired; until that succeeds, the task remains SUSPENDED and performs no work step. onResumed indicates a return to execution after this process, not the creation of a new logical task.

The current executor limits task payloads to 64 KiB, each resource payload to 8 KiB, tracked reservations to 16, and the total frame to 128 KiB. These implementation limits encourage compact state. For unknown types or malformed persisted state, the runtime retains the original frame without executing unknown code; recovery requires the appropriate type and another decode attempt.

A completion callback should not be the only place where a long-running operation issues an irreversible reward. The server can stop between an external side effect and persistence of the task. Use operation IDs and the request ledger for deliveries; for custom operations, persist an explicit completion stage and make recovery idempotent.

Reserving Work Targets

A robotics resource is not necessarily an item. RobotResource may represent a target block, station, work area, or external quota. RobotResourceRequest(resource, amount) requires a positive amount; RobotResourceLease exposes its owner, resource, granted amount, active(), and close().

java
Optional<RobotResourceLease> claim = context.acquire(
    new RobotResourceRequest(new BlockRobotResource(target), 1)
);
if (claim.isEmpty()) {
    return new RobotTaskResult(
        RobotTaskResult.Status.RETRY, "target_busy"
    );
}

BlockRobotResource stores a position and optional side. The built-in block reservation type accepts only an amount of 1 and uses the existing robotics registry to prevent two robots from claiming the same target at once. This reserves work; it does not prohibit a player from modifying the block or authorize a robot to break it.

Do not reacquire the same reservation needlessly on every tick: the executor tracks issued leases, so that could exhaust its limit. Keep the active lease in temporary runtime state or acquire it at a phase transition. After recovery, follow the reacquisition contract rather than serializing the Java lease object.

For a custom resource, register RobotResourceType<R>(id, resourceClass, persistence, acquirer). RobotResourceAcquirer.acquire(Level, robotId, resource, amount) must return an active lease or an empty result. Repeated close calls must be safe, and an old lease must not clear a reservation subsequently acquired by another robot.

Leases issued during task execution are associated with the executor and released at completion. External code calling RobotService.acquire outside a task callback must manage lease lifetimes itself. Tracking also requires correctly serializing the registered resource; an unserializable resource does not become a durable reservation just because active() exists.

Docks and Requests

RobotService.dock(level, pos) finds a dock without a side, while the overload with Direction finds a side-specific dock. For a pipe plug, the side forms part of its address, so do not always substitute null. RobotDock exposes position, side, occupancy, and typed ports.

BuildCraftDockPorts provides ITEMS, FLUIDS, MJ, and EXTERNAL_ENERGY keys. dock.port(type) returns an available capability, not a promise that every dock supports everything. Built-in item and fluid wrappers respect dock settings. A custom DockPortType<T> has an ID, Class<T>, and DockPortResolver<T> receiving a RobotDockContext with world, position, side, and occupancy. Register the type through ContentRegistrar.dockPort; a locally created key with an unknown ID does not connect a port.

For logistics, RobotTaskContext.reserveRequest, cancelRequest, and deliverRequest pass the task owner to the request service. Delivery uses a reservation ID and delivery ID, preserving duplicate-delivery suppression. RequestLedger defines the full lifecycle of those identifiers; moving the robot and retaining ownership of the carried stack are still responsibilities of your program.

Events: Use Verified Hook Points

Register RobotEventListener in ROBOT_EVENT_LISTENERS to receive RobotEventContext: event kind, robot, world, optional actor, and a defensive copy of the held item. Decisions combine as DENY > ALLOW > PASS; denial stops iteration. The current implementation orders listeners by registration ID.

RobotEventKind includes spawn, place, interact, dismantle, docking, and task events. In the standard BCCE 8.0.24 implementation, dispatch calls are wired for PLACE, INTERACT, and DISMANTLE. The presence of TASK_STARTED, TASK_FINISHED, TASK_FAILED, SPAWN, DOCK, and UNDOCK in the enum does not guarantee their automatic dispatch. Use RobotTaskLifecycle for custom tasks; do not make critical behavior depend on unwired events.

IV. World, Robots, and Presentation

28Plants and Resource Generation

A robot should understand a crop through its behavior, while a resource generator should select worlds through an explicit rule. These extensions solve different problems: CropAdapter participates in existing robot actions, whereas ResourceDepositRule controls how an existing world-generation profile applies.

Making a Crop Available to Robots

CropAdapter defines seed recognition, planting checks, planting itself, maturity checks, and harvesting. Register it through CropService.register(id, priority, adapter); adapters() lists CropRegistration entries. Higher-priority adapters are checked first; equal priorities are ordered by ID.

Answer five questions when designing an adapter:

MethodExpected Behavior
isSeed(ItemStack)Pure check whether an item can be used as a seed.
canSustainPlant(Level, seed, pos)Check the planting location without consuming a seed or modifying the world.
plant(Level, Player, seed, pos)Perform planting on behalf of the supplied player.
isMature(BlockGetter, state, pos)Pure check whether the block is ready for harvest.
harvest(Level, pos, NonNullList<ItemStack> drops, Player)Perform harvesting and return drops through the supplied list.

In the built-in planting path, pos identifies the supporting block where the robot uses the seed; the plant usually occupies pos.above(). During harvesting, pos identifies the plant itself. Confusing these coordinates makes the robot recognize seeds correctly while continually rejecting suitable farmland.

java
BuildCraftApi.service(BuildCraftServices.CROPS)
    .register(bc.id("orchard_crop"), 200, orchardAdapter);

orchardAdapter implements all five methods. Both the service and built-in planter/harvester use this contract. Set priority so your crop-specific logic runs before a generic handler while recognizing only crops it owns.

For planting, the service checks isSeed, then canSustainPlant, and finally calls plant. For harvesting, it first checks maturity and passes a separate copy of the drops list. Only a successful harvest commits changes to the list. If a harvester throws, the runtime stops harvesting instead of handing a potentially modified block to another adapter. Returning false may continue the search, so reject a crop before modifying it.

The drops list is the sole harvest result for an ordinary robot; the robot itself ejects the returned items. If an adapter both adds a stack to drops and spawns it in the world, items are duplicated. Likewise, decide who consumes the seed exactly once. The built-in planter additionally consumes one item if the successful handler left the stack count unchanged. This safeguard applies to the robot path, not every external call to CropService.plant.

CropAdapter has no simulation mode. isSeed, canSustainPlant, and isMature must be pure; do not call plant or harvest just to check feasibility. Built-in robots check permissions before changing the world, but a direct external service call does not inherit a robot's authority. Use the supplied Player when interacting with protection rules and the crop's own semantics.

Enabling a Built-In Resource in a Custom Dimension

ResourceDepositRule contains a rule ID, generation-profile ID, WorldTargetSelector, frequency multiplier, priority, and enabled flag. Register it through WorldgenService.register(rule, RegistrationContext) or ContentRegistrar.worldgen(rule).

java
bc.worldgen(ResourceDepositRule.builder(
        bc.id("moon_oil"), BuildCraftContentIds.Worldgen.STANDARD_OIL)
    .target(WorldTargetSelector.builder()
        .dimension(bc.id("moon"))
        .biomeTag(bc.id("oil_bearing"))
        .excludeBiome(bc.id("protected_crater"))
        .build())
    .frequencyMultiplier(0.5)
    .priority(100)
    .build());

For simple cases, use bc.oilInDimension(path, dimension) or its multiplier overload. The rule format is suitable for data-driven definitions, but this Java registration does not by itself install a datapack format or create a new generator.

WorldTargetSelector separately specifies included dimensions, dimension-type tags, excluded dimensions, biomes, biome tags, and excluded biomes. An empty inclusion set means all. Within each group, an ID or tag match is sufficient; between the dimension and biome groups, both must match. Exclusions always win. The oil-generation runtime checks dimension tags against DIMENSION_TYPE, not an arbitrary collection of dimension keys.

The service stores rules sorted by descending priority and then ID. Its working consumer in BCCE 8.0.24 is OilGenFeature, which selects the first enabled matching rule for the BuildCraftContentIds.Worldgen.STANDARD_OIL profile. This is connected to the platform world-generation path, not just a registered descriptor. The API does not, however, expose a public registry of arbitrary generators for any new profile.

Account for the following behavior of the current implementation:

  • A multiplier of 0 suppresses the generation attempt; values between 0 and 1 probabilistically reduce the number of attempts.

  • Values above 1 perform the same attempt as a multiplier of 1; they currently do not create additional deposits. The field's name is not a guarantee of linearly increased frequency.

  • A rule with enabled(false) is excluded from selection; it does not block a matching lower-priority rule. To suppress generation in an area using this mechanism, register a high-priority enabled rule with a multiplier of 0.

  • The global oil-generation setting and dimension restrictions from the configuration still apply.

Registering a rule changes future generation attempts. It does not request retrogen in already generated chunks or modify existing deposits. For diagnosis, check that Energy is loaded, dimension and biome IDs, the selected rule, and configuration before investigating the deposit's shape.

IV. World, Robots, and Presentation

29Integration Items: Tools, Maps, Facades, and Drops

This part of the API connects an addon's existing content to BuildCraft's gameplay interactions. Usually, you only need to register an adapter with a precise applicability check. There is no need to extend BCCE's internal map item, wrench, or facade classes.

Rotating and Painting Blocks

BlockInteractionService accepts a RotationContext or PaintContext and returns a structured result. Contexts include world, position, block state, owner, and OperationMode. Rotation also receives a face; painting receives a color, hit position, and optional side.

PaintContext.color() == null has a specific meaning: remove the paint. It is not invalid input. Hit position and side matter for composite objects, notably pipes with attachments. The compatibility shorthand constructor uses the block center and no side, so pass the full context when the hit position is known.

Register RotationHandler in ROTATION_HANDLERS and PaintHandler in PAINT_HANDLERS. A handler returns PASS for an unrelated block, ROTATED / PAINTED on success, DENIED when prohibited, or FAILED on failure. The first non-PASS result ends dispatch. Do not use FAILED to mean “this is not my block”: that would suppress the standard fallback.

On the server, the dispatcher first checks chunk availability, BLOCK_INTERACT permission, and the interaction event. The custom callback must still honor SIMULATE. The legacy built-in rotation and painting handlers run only for EXECUTE; if their behavior cannot be safely predicted, simulation returns PASS rather than falsely claiming that the operation is impossible.

Supporting a Custom Wrench

WrenchService.isWrench(ItemStack) only recognizes wrench items. Integrate your own item through WrenchAdapter.recognizes(stack) and optional onUsed(WrenchUseContext) notification.

java
bc.wrench("service_wrench", new WrenchAdapter() {
    @Override public boolean recognizes(ItemStack stack) {
        return stack.is(serviceWrenchItem);
    }

    @Override public void onUsed(WrenchUseContext context) {
        // Начислите износ или обновите состояние вашего инструмента.
        // Callback относится к уже успешно обработанному действию.
    }
});

serviceWrenchItem is an item registered by the addon. WrenchUseContext supplies the player, hand, actual stack, and hit result. The stack is deliberately not a defensive copy, so the adapter can account for tool usage. The built-in bridge notifies all adapters that recognize the stack, so two overlapping handlers can both apply durability loss. Keep recognition conditions narrow.

The runtime also recognizes internal BuildCraft wrenches and, when enabled in configuration, the c:tools/wrench tag. The tag is suitable for simple recognition; use an adapter for special post-use behavior.

WrenchContext is a separate public container for side, tool, owner, and mode. However, the current WrenchService has no use(WrenchContext) method or universal wrench-based rotation command. Use BlockInteractionService for the actual operation; do not design an integration around a nonexistent method.

Item Labels

ItemLabelAdapter defines supports(stack), label(stack), and setLabel(stack, label, mode). Implement it directly in the item class or register it in ITEM_LABEL_ADAPTERS. The current service checks direct item implementations first, followed by registered adapters.

java
ItemLabelService labels = BuildCraftApi.service(BuildCraftServices.ITEM_LABELS);
Optional<String> oldLabel = labels.label(stack);
boolean accepted = labels.setLabel(stack, "Северный склад", OperationMode.EXECUTE);

A label should reflect the item's own adapter-managed content, not an arbitrary field in someone else's NBT. requireLabel checks support and a non-null string reference, but permits the empty string as a value. Unlike the map service, ItemLabelService does not substitute a stack copy for simulation: the setLabel(..., SIMULATE) implementation itself must be pure. Global registration does not authorize an addon to rename another mod's server-side stack based on an unchecked client request.

Custom Map-Location Carriers

MapLocationAdapter converts an item stack to and from a semantic MapLocationView. Its methods are supports, read, write, and clear. Implement it in the item or register it in MAP_LOCATION_ADAPTERS, including through ContentRegistrar.mapLocationAdapter.

MapLocationKind distinguishes CLEAN, SPOT, AREA, PATH, ZONE, and PATH_REPEATING. MapLocationView contains a label and optional geometry views; common cases have point, box, zone, path, repeatingPath, and clean factories.

java
MapLocationView destination = MapLocationView.point(
    "Разгрузка", stationPos, Direction.NORTH
);
MapLocationService maps = BuildCraftApi.service(BuildCraftServices.MAP_LOCATIONS);
if (maps.write(stack, destination, OperationMode.SIMULATE)) {
    boolean written = maps.write(stack, destination, OperationMode.EXECUTE);
    // Обработайте written: симуляция не резервирует состояние предмета.
}

The service reads a copy of the stack and, for simulated writes or clearing, passes a copy to the adapter. An adapter exception becomes an absent result or false. Actual execution mutates the supplied stack, so the caller must own it and synchronize it through the normal mechanisms.

CLEAN must have no geometry. For other kinds, use appropriate factories and validate consistency of persisted fields in your codec. MapLocationView is a stable semantic representation, but arbitrary Path and Zone implementations remain responsible for immutability and serialization. Zone does not supply a universal codec for any Java predicate.

This bridge is used by markers, the Zone Planner, map visualization, and robot actions. A custom item can thus carry a point, region, or route without impersonating a specific built-in item class. It does not create movement automatically: the map supplies data, while the consumer chooses the action.

Facade Materials and Phases

FacadeService.resolve(BlockState) and resolve(ItemStack) identify facade materials through FacadeMaterialAdapter. FacadeStateResult contains FacadeMaterial(state, transparent) and the source item, copied when read. source() is empty when no representative item exists.

Create a phased facade through createPhased(List<FacadePhase>, boolean hollow). Each phase defines a block state and active color. activeColour == null means an uncolored phase. The current service allows between one and seventeen phases; a color may appear only once, and an uncolored phase is allowed once.

java
Optional<ItemStack> facade = BuildCraftApi
    .service(BuildCraftServices.FACADES)
    .createPhased(List.of(
        new FacadePhase(Blocks.STONE.defaultBlockState(), null),
        new FacadePhase(Blocks.GLASS.defaultBlockState(), DyeColor.BLUE)
    ), false);

Success depends on whether the materials exist in the built-in facade collection. The normal backend uses its existing phased-item codec. An addon can provide its own FacadeMaterialAdapter, but returning an unrelated item, as the minimal stub in MiscParityFixtureAddon does, is useful only for testing the call, not for working gameplay.

FacadeRuleService operates at the material-discovery level: disable(ruleId, Block, provenance) excludes a block, and mapState(ruleId, BlockState, ItemStack, provenance) provides an item for a particular state. disabledBy and mappedStack reveal the chosen result. Rule IDs must be unique; conflicting mappings resolve by provenance priority and, on ties, deterministically by ID. An empty stack is invalid for mapState.

An item mapping does not make arbitrary geometry a valid facade: the built-in discoverer separately checks fluids, block entities, shape, and model type. Do not change rules after the cache has been built and expect all items to be rebuilt automatically: the public interface promises no such refresh operation.

Converting Stored Fluids into Item Drops

FluidDropProvider.createDrops(FluidDropContext) creates item representations of fluid volume without relying on loader-specific FluidStack types. The context contains FluidVolume and optional Level; use FluidDropContext.of(volume) when no world is available.

The FLUID_DROPS service aggregates results from all registered providers. This differs from a “first applicable handler wins” chain. If two providers both return a full volume of the same fluid, the result is doubled. Providers must restrict their applicability clearly and coordinate with other fluid-representation rules.

Return nonempty stacks; the service filters null and empty entries and makes defensive copies. The call only creates a drop description: it does not pour fluid into the world, reduce the source tank, or spawn items. The invoking game mechanism must connect the result to one-time removal of the fluid. Because the context may not include a world, never use context.level().get() without checking it.

IV. World, Robots, and Presentation

30Content Presentation and the In-Game Guide

BCCE's public presentation layer defines resource identifiers, labels, and synchronized visual values. An addon can tell the client how to display its content without sending server components into the renderer or extending an internal renderer.

Registering a model or menu does not automatically create a Minecraft block entity renderer, screen, or network protocol. Built-in pipes already consume presentation metadata. For a custom block, the addon still implements its loader's normal client integration and uses the public presentation data as input.

Describing Static Appearance

ContentPresentation contains the content ID, title key, optional description, icon ID, and model ID. PipePresentation adds texture layers. StatementPresentation describes a condition/action label and icon. ParameterPresentation adds an ID for the parameter-editor type.

These records do not import net.minecraft.client. They may be constructed in common code, provided your own classes do not reference client-only types either. The package is called client because the data is intended for presentation, not because it is an instruction to load a screen on a dedicated server.

java
ResourceLocation typeId = bc.id("visual_pipe");
ContentPresentation base = new ContentPresentation(
    typeId, "example.pipe.visual", "example.pipe.visual.description",
    bc.id("gui/visual_pipe"), bc.id("block/visual_pipe")
);
BuildCraftApi.registry(BuildCraftRegistries.PIPE_PRESENTATIONS)
    .register(typeId, new PipePresentation(base, List.of()), () -> "example");

Identifiers must correspond to actual addon resources. A model ID refers to a model resource; pipe layers refer to sprites that must enter the relevant atlas through normal asset registration. A string in presentation metadata does not create a file or guarantee that it will load.

ClientPresentationService provides presentation(contentId), pipe(typeId), statement(id), parameter(id), and menu(contentId) lookups. Missing metadata is returned as an Optional. Use an intelligible fallback in your UI rather than allowing a NullPointerException.

Selecting Models from Synchronized State

DynamicPresentation has optional pipe(PipeView, partialTick), machine(MachineExecutionContext, partialTick), and engine(EngineHost, partialTick) selectors. They operate on client representations. Read required values from typed presentation channels, not mutable server components.

Every model a selector might return must be declared ahead of time in models(). The current runtime collects these during model setup, before baking. Returning a newly invented model ID from a render callback is too late: models should not be baked on a render or chunk-mesh thread.

java
final class PipeLook implements DynamicPresentation {
    private final ResourceLocation idle =
        ResourceLocation.tryParse("example:block/pipe_idle");
    private final ResourceLocation active =
        ResourceLocation.tryParse("example:block/pipe_active");
    private final ResourceLocation strength =
        ResourceLocation.tryParse("example:strength");

    @Override public Set<ResourceLocation> models() {
        return Set.of(idle, active);
    }

    @Override public Optional<PresentationFrame> pipe(
            PipeView view, float partialTick) {
        int value = view.presentation(strength, Integer.class).orElse(0);
        return Optional.of(new PresentationFrame(
            value > 0 ? active : idle,
            List.of(), Map.of(), null, null
        ));
    }
}

BuildCraftApi.registry(BuildCraftRegistries.DYNAMIC_PRESENTATIONS)
    .register(typeId, new PipeLook(), () -> "example");

The example assumes that the example:strength channel is already defined and its value delivered by a component through its synchronization contract. The selector itself does not perform synchronization. PresentationConformanceAddon illustrates reading such a channel for pipes and machines; the example above also explicitly declares dynamic models, which is necessary for rendering them.

PresentationFrame contains a model, up to 32 texture layers, up to 64 animation channels, an optional sound, and a menu. Each animation value must be finite and within [0, 1]. The service also validates partialTick against that range. Normalize progress and handle division by a zero-duration operation before building a frame.

frame.over(base) inherits missing model, sound, and menu, uses the base layers when the new list is empty, and merges animations with the new value taking precedence. Thus an empty layer list means inheritance; null is not an instruction to forcibly remove the base sound.

The built-in service adds buildcraft:work_progress for machines and buildcraft:engine_piston, buildcraft:engine_heat, and synchronized sound for engines. Selector errors fall back to an available static frame with diagnostics rather than breaking the entire renderer.

Understanding Which Channels Actually Animate

An arbitrary animation ID is data that a consumer must interpret. Existing shared model rendering supports buildcraft:offset_x, offset_y, offset_z and rotation_x, rotation_y, rotation_z under the same namespace. Offsets are interpreted as value - 0.5; rotations as value × 360° about the origin of the model's coordinate system.

A channel named example:movement will not move a model merely because its value exists in a map. A custom renderer can consume it, or a selector can convert it to the supported buildcraft:rotation_y. work_progress, temperature, and piston phase likewise have meaning for their respective consumers; they do not define universal skeletal animation.

For addon machines, public frame(machine, partialTick) and frame(engine, partialTick) methods are available. Use their result in the addon's normal renderer. Do not import buildcraft.lib.client.render.ApiPresentationModels for this purpose: it is a BCCE implementation class, outside the supported api.v2 surface.

Menus and Actions

MenuPresentation(menuId, titleKey, actions) describes a menu and at most 64 ActionPresentation entries. An action has an ID, title key, and optional icon. These metadata help label buttons consistently and describe which actions a UI exposes.

They contain no arbitrary executable callbacks and do not authorize the client to execute actions. Actual menus/screens are registered through the Minecraft loader; the server handler must revalidate the target, actor, distance, and permitted action. If you use the machine-menu bridge, consult the machine chapter. An actionId appearing in a client frame is not sufficient authorization.

Adding Guide Book Content

The Guide Book accepts sections and entries as common data. GuideSection has an ID, title key, optional icon and parent, and sort order. A GuideEntry references a section and has its own title, icon, order, and nonempty list of pages.

java
ResourceLocation sectionId = bc.id("logistics");
ResourceLocation entryId = bc.id("inspection_robot");

bc.guideSection(GuideSection.builder(
        sectionId, "example.guide.logistics")
    .order(100)
    .build());

bc.guideEntry(GuideEntry.builder(
        entryId, sectionId, "example.guide.inspection_robot")
    .order(10)
    .page(GuidePages.textKey("example.guide.inspection_robot.overview"))
    .page(GuidePages.recipe(bc.id("inspection_board")))
    .page(GuidePages.image(
        bc.id("textures/gui/guide/inspection_robot.png"), 128, 96,
        "example.guide.inspection_robot.diagram"
    ))
    .build());

Five standard GuidePage variants are available directly and through GuidePages:

  • Text — literal text/markup or a translation key. textKey stores the key; the client performs translation.

  • Recipe — a recipe ID; the built-in renderer resolves the recipe through supported recipe presentation.

  • Image — a texture resource, positive width and height, and optional caption.

  • Link — a labeled navigation link to another entry ID.

  • Item — an item with supporting text; the current renderer also displays its recipes and uses.

The built-in implementation inserts a page break between supplied pages. Do not duplicate an entry's title at the beginning of its first text page: the guide structure already renders it. Sections and entries sort by ascending order, then ID.

GuideService supports fetching individual sections and entries, listing them all, and listing entries in a given section. Java registration supplies an owner; duplicate IDs are rejected with the previous owner reported. Empty titles and entries without pages are invalid. When nesting sections or linking entries, check that targets exist: a parent or targetEntry field does not guarantee the target has been registered.

The built-in renderer supports exactly these GuidePage.Text, Recipe, Image, Link, and Item variants. The fact that GuidePage is an interface does not imply an extension point for an arbitrary sixth renderer. For portable content, use the standard variants and addon assets.

V. Maintenance

31Diagnosing and Validating Integrations

Validate an addon by starting with dependencies and data, then testing actual gameplay behavior. These levels prove different things: compilation establishes that signatures exist and match, but cannot create a backend where only a descriptor is registered.

Diagnostic Data

ApiDiagnostics exposes INFO, WARNING, and ERROR messages. The current runtime installs a mutable backend, but the common interface also allows read-only views: its default report throws UnsupportedOperationException. Treat messages as API information; do not assume every returned view permits writing.

DebugService collects sections from registered DebugContributor instances. DebugContext provides the world, position, optional side, and client mode. DebugSection contains a title and lines of technical information; it is a developer-tool format, not a localized in-game GUI. A contributor should collect state quickly without changing it or retaining the supplied context after the call.

For registration failures, inspect ID, owner, and lifecycle. For data failures, inspect generation, provenance, the winning definition, and rejection reason. For resource transfers, record offered amount, actual result, remainder, port side, and mode. For permission failures, record actor, operation, authority, and reason. Such a report helps reproduce the cause rather than just saying “the API does not work.”

Testkit

TestApiRuntime is a small in-memory runtime. You can add the registries and services needed by a test, set its version and features, and transition test registries to FROZEN. It does not install itself globally or initialize BCCE modules. Production code accepting ApiRuntime or specific services as parameters is straightforward to test in this environment.

TestExtensionContext holds values under ContextKey entries. put checks that the Java value matches the key's type, and get returns a typed Optional. This supports testing callbacks with and without a published PIPE, MACHINE, or other view.

The testkit does not emulate the entire game bootstrap. For example, setting lifecycle in a test runtime does not create a world, freeze arbitrary addon services, or initialize native capabilities. A passing test confirms only behavior that was actually modeled.

Checking Addon Compatibility

Compile addon code against BCCE's public classes without putting internal implementation packages on its compile classpath. Then test the assembled JAR with the actual dependencies for the target Minecraft version and loader. Successful compilation confirms correct signatures, not working gameplay.

Choose game tests based on the extension's responsibilities. Storage needs partial transfers and no mutation during simulation. A persistent component needs load, unload, and unknown-payload tests. A new renderer needs client and dedicated-server tests. World operations need permission-denial and resource-ownership tests. A runtime host needs tick, save, and unregister-on-unload tests. Testing unrelated scenarios does not replace testing your own contract.

Common Failure Causes

SymptomWhat to Check
service(...) is emptyIs the corresponding module loaded and its backend installed?
Registry reports duplicate IDIs registration called twice, or is the ID/alias already owned by another extension?
Registry is already frozenWas registration deferred until load-complete, first tick, or reload?
Type exists, but block does nothingDoes it have an executable factory/handler wired to its host?
Simulation succeeds, execution transfers zeroAre you using the default ALL_OR_NOTHING, or did the storage change?
Items are lost after a failed transferWhere is the unaccepted remainder stored, and who owns it between operations?
Data did not updateCheck published(), attempt diagnostics, and the active snapshot's generation.
Addon works only in the IDEDoes it import internal implementations, or does the production JAR not match its target environment?
Server crashes during startupWere client-only classes loaded by the addon's common bootstrap?

V. Maintenance

32Migrating an Addon from the Original API

In BCCE API 2.1, the old public buildcraft.api.* packages outside buildcraft.api.v2 are no longer supported. Some historical classes exist in internal packages for BCCE's own operation. Importing those implementations is not a supported compatibility strategy for the old API.

BCCE API 2.1 is not binary-compatible with addons compiled against the original API. Even if a similar implementation exists inside BCCE, the old import or method call may fail. Port addons to the public buildcraft.api.v2 contracts.

Migration Map

Original Integration ApproachNew Extension PointWhat Must Be Reconsidered
BuildcraftFuelRegistryEnergyFluidService, fuel and coolant profilesUnits, matchers, definition IDs, provenance
BuildcraftRecipeRegistry and domain recipe managersMachineRecipeService, typed definitionsCounted ingredients, item components, outputs, recipe sources
MjAPI capabilities, IMjReceiver, MjBatteryEnergyService, MjPort, MjStorage, platform portsResult semantics, requested/accepted/remainder, port lifecycle
PipeDefinition, PipeBehaviour subclassPipeType, routing/connection components, or PipeBehaviourDefinitionInstance factory, scoped context, state persistence
PipeFlow subclass and direct holder accessPipeFlowDefinition, PipeView, domain-specific transport servicesAdmission, traveling-item ownership, synchronization and persistence
PipePluggablePipeAttachmentType and attachment instancesSide, ports, model, installation/removal, unknown state
StatementManager, IStatementParameterTriggerType, ActionType, ParameterTypeSchema, codec, ordered contributors, client presentation
Direct wire APISignalService, SignalChannelType, Boolean channelsActual channel backend, signal source, lifetime
AIRobot, boards, and ResourceIdRobotTaskType, RobotTask, board programs, typed resourcesTask lifecycle, leases, docking, state migration
Schematic subclasses and handlersSchematicAdapter, snapshot elements, placement contextSeparate capture and placement, resource consumption, permissions, inventory copy
Global template/filler registriesTemplateService, FillerPatternTypeReturned result, orientation, and actual caller parameters
IToolWrench, rotation/paint hooksWrench and block-interaction services/adaptersItem support separate from action and resource consumption
Mutable item lists and facade registriesItem-list and facade APIMatching mode, components, materials/phases, rule sources
FakePlayer providerAutomationActor and permission contextOwner provenance, target, operation kind, handling PASS / DENY
Arbitrary API network callbacksDomain-specific typed synchronization and presentationPermitted payload, direction, and lifecycle

This table maps the direction of migration, not mechanical name substitution. An old class may split into a type descriptor, component, codec, and view. Conversely, several former access points may converge into one service.

Migration Procedure

First, separate the addon's shared gameplay logic from loader code, client rendering, and BCCE internal references. Record what the addon actually does: filters items, creates an energy endpoint, adds robot work, or changes appearance. For each operation, choose the narrowest suitable contract from the migration map.

Next, migrate stable IDs and data. Map old names to new ones, define codecs and migrations, and test unknown payloads. Do not rename persisted IDs and change their format simultaneously without an explicit transition. Preserving old saves and maintaining binary compatibility with the old Java API are different problems.

Then connect the runtime: register the type, factories, and callbacks; create or locate a host; establish tick/unload order; and identify the owner of resources. Confirm that the chosen backend actually invokes your contract. If an execution hook is missing, a descriptor or feature flag is no substitute.

Add client models, GUI, and synchronization through the appropriate presentation contracts. Test a dedicated server to ensure common addon bootstrap does not load client-only classes. Finally, build and test gameplay on each target platform, including partial operations, denied permissions, and loading old saves. Preserve gameplay semantics during migration—including balance, transport intervals, and robot behavior; changing the API contract does not automatically require changing game mechanics.

Each constant is a RegistryKey<T>; T specifies the values accepted by its ApiRegistry<T>. Registries store extension descriptors or adapters. Features and Contract Levels

All BuildCraftFeatures constants are ResourceLocation values. The runtime assigns a level when creating each ApiFeature. The table gives levels from the shared runtime, matching the effective 26.X/NeoForge implementation. A level does not indicate Minecraft version or completeness of gameplay behavior. Supplement feature checks by obtaining the required service and testing the supported object.
